review:
This review comes from someone who bought the game three and a half years ago, and has tried (unsuccessfully) around 11 times to beat the game, only for me to drop the game mid way through the first act, every time. Until a couple weeks ago, when I finally beat the game.

What changed? My perception and my understanding of the game, as well as the amount of patience I gave to it. If you have problems with games that start slow, and if dumping massive amounts of lore from the get go is a turn off for you, read on because I found a way to power through that.

[list]
[*] [b]This is the most important tip I can give you.[/b] The first act of the game is kinda slow, meandering, and doesn't really move the plot forward. I promise you this, the second act is an order of magnitude better than the first act. The third act starts weak, but it picks up really fast and it gets REAL GOOD. If you think this game has potential like I did, but you keep getting kinda bored, trust me, just get to the second act, it's 100% worth it. The second act starts when you get to [spoiler]Defiance Bay.[/spoiler]

[*] At the start of the game, you get to create your character and have a myriad of different options to choose from. Don't worry about making the "wrong" decision, you'd be hard pressed to make an unviable character, let alone such a disaster of a character that makes you unable to beat the game. You get 5 other party members aside from the one that you created who are pretty good early on, and complete beasts later on. Not only that, there's a "retrain" option readily available everywhere in the game, that allows you to re-spec everything (except Stats). 

[*] For stats, follow the in-game guide, which is the little stars next to the Stats that say [b]RECOMMENDED[/b] and [b]HIGHLY RECOMMENDED[/b]. My advice would be, and this is not a story spoiler, rather a mechanical one: [spoiler]to not increase any Stat past 16, since it's laughably easy to get bonuses that get you up to 19~20, and the highest conversation Stat check is 18. You can safely disregard the previous advice and allot your points into anything as high as you want, the character I beat the game with started with 20 Strength, and it was a ridiculous overkill for stat checks, but the damage bonus was really nice.[/spoiler] 

[*] I don't know if I'm alone in this, but considering the game references a bunch regions and their borders with each other, I would have liked to have a map to have an idea where they are exactly. To me, this helps a lot, I don't know why. [url=https://s3.amazonaws.com/uploads.forums.obsidian.net/monthly_01_2017/post-52304-0-52048600-1485175789.png]Here's a link to the map of the entire world in the game[/url] (this really isn't a spoiler, it's just to get you an idea)

[*] Be patient and read through the books you find, even the ones you think are pointless. Trust me, they are not and most of them are referenced in some way by NPCs. This helped me understand how the world inside the game worked. The only ones I disregarded were the ones with poems, but that's up to you, really. Also, you'll eventually read them all, there aren't that many, and  some of them (the history ones) usually explain the exact same event from a different point of view, so it's a really easy read.

[*] The game pretty much gives you 2 party members for free really early on, and you can tackle a couple quests shortly after that. My suggestion is that you avoid the quests for just a moment, and get yourself more party members fast. Having less that 6 party members is a BIG disadvantage though you don't need all 6, and you can easily get an extra one by just exploring outside of Gilded Vale (the first town), specifically [spoiler]Magran's Fork[/spoiler] . You can also create a second custom character in an inn early on (super cheap) and fill your party while you find yourself another [i]real[/i] party member. It's worth it.

[*] I also suggest that you designate a character to train Mechanics, which is a skill that allows you to deal with locked storages, and detect and disable traps. There's never not a dungeon without a locked storage and a dozen traps, it's for your own good really. What I did was use the ability to create a second custom character and made it my Mechanics character, though, you don't need to do this, any will do.

[*] Last but not least, don't be afraid to equip characters whose class archetype doesn't use a certain kind of equipment. For example, a wizard with a two handed sword? Sure. A priest in heavy armor? OK. A ranger with a staff? Why not. You should equip your characters to satisfy your needs, not to fit some hypothetical mold in some other game, where wearing armor as a wizard made your spells suck. In general, having armor (that is, Damage Reduction) is way better than any benefit you might get from not having armor (there are exceptions, feel free to experiment, considering my priest never changed his robe, but my ranger had heavy plate). Enemies in Pillars are not that dumb and tend to attack characters who the game knows are weak. If they are no longer weak, it doesn't matter as much if they get attacked.
[/list]

In conclusion, Pillars has an agonizing start, but pays off around mid game, and it never drops the ball after that.

I noticed that most people reviewing this game have previously played similar games. I don't have much experience with CRPG'S at all, thats why I thought my view of the game can give another perspective on things. That means I have not played games like Dungeons & Dragons, Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale or Neverwinter Nights before playing this game.

Pillars of Eternity starts of with a character creation. The amount of options that you have here is absolutely crazy. You can probably spend hours here, changing every little detail. You pick your sex, race, class, attributes, culture, appearance and finally voice.

This game have many difficult settings and are obviously made for replayability. Pillars recommend that you start on easy difficulty, so I did. I most say that easy in this game isn't that simple! 

Loadscreens while you rest are pretty and some other environments in the game, like dungeons and forests. I like the details on the characters, it's very sharp, even when you zoom in. The only complaint I have is that some backgrounds are a little blurry and low res, which looks a little bit silly when it's next to a very detailed character. I get that they went for an "old-school look" but I still think that doesnt really match. But when you zoom out that won't really bother you.

I recommend that you crank the volume up for this title, because background noise and sounds, in the dialogue and in combat, are great. It will help you get into the story and atmosphere better.

Ventors in the cities and villages will buy all the trash you loot from enemies. You can buy camping tools, weapons and potions from them. If you have many followers you can carry more items, and all items can be transfered over between anybody in your party, which is great. So if I find a staff as barbarian I can simply open up the inventory and equip in on my mage.

You will have to read most of the dialogue yourself, although some story related things are read for you. I still wouldn't recommend this game if you hate reading, because there's a lot of it. You can right click on items and spells to read everything about them as well. Some are just lore stuff, others are actually useful information.

The story is dark and mysterious. Combat in done with real time and pause. You can also use slow motion in fights to make things more manageable and easy. As you level up your character and possible followers, you gain points which you can spend on things like sneak, survival, etc. You also get to pick spells.

You can create really silly partys if you want. You can combine all the races and even have animal followers like bears. It's entirely up to you who you bring along the quests and you can choose how they will look like, what weapon they will use and what role they will have in combat.

Options menu is very good. You can customize everything they way you like it in terms of controls. The graphics options are not as good, but for this type of game I wouldn't say its needed.

The replayability is obviously insane when you think about how many races, followers and difficulty levels this game has. You can play the entire game solo, or you can choose to bring mages, dwarfs, godlikes, wizards, humans...and so on, with you. You can also create different kinds of humans, elfs, etc. It's fantastic.

Obsidian Entertainment has created a great game overall, that even new CRPG players like me can enjoy. I have barely scratched the surface of this game, but I can already see that amount of work put into this title.
 It's fun, dark and mysterious and im having so much fun playing and learning new things everyday.
Highly recommended title, if you don't mind reading of course.

I realize this is an older game, but I love games like this! I admit I'm using a walkthrough; I just wish there was one for all the side quests and tasks!! Some are easy enough but several are not. (My excuse is that I'm over 60 yrs old and it's difficult to remember things Ha-Ha!)

Pillars of Eternity is an isometric party-based computer RPG using real-time-with-pause combat.

What is Great about this game:

- Complex and deep story that moves the game along incredibly well
- Deep character creation and multiple classes each with multiple viable playstyles bringing significant variety to your own playthrough
- Rich and appropriate back story, lore, and flavor text added throughout the game that is worth reading
- Enjoyable tactical combat with numerous options for pausing and other options to make the game more enjoyable
- Unique and sometimes fascinating quest lines with multiple alternative methods for success (e.g. talk yourself out of a combat encounter)
- An ending storyline that was possibly the most thought-provoking and intelligently written as any I have experienced

What is Good about this game:

- The game looks quite nice but could have used more art/animantions to improve it further
- The voice acting is quite good where it exists
- Good use of Steam features (cloud saves, trading cards, achievements, etc)

What is Bad about this game:

- The combat could have been significantly improved (although still very good) by including methods to automate companions similar to the systems in FFXII or Dragon Age: Origins
- Given how story heavy this game is, it would have been much improved by including more voice-over work.  The voice acting is very good, but is only available sparsely.  The writing is more than worth reading, but having it spoken would have been that much more engrossing.

Conclusion:

Pillars of Eternity is the current pinnacle of story-telling in RPGs with a great combat system and a classic style.

9.5 / 10.0

It's hard not to compare this with Divinity: Original Sin. Both were funded on Kickstarter, both have a 91% score on Steam, both are rich, engaging cRPGs, and they were released months apart. It's fair to say both games have been wild successes that have surprised even the developers. If you had to pick ONE of these to invest time in which should it be?

Turn-based vs. Real-time with pause: I eventually came to accept and even enjoy the real-time with pause combat of Pillars, though I much prefer turn-based. Real-time combat presents many problems that aren't the result of player mistakes. On numerous occasions I'd have characters stuck in place because the pathfinding didn't work right. The real-time combat often felt like a jumbled, chaotic mess instead of the tactical plan I had set out. Divinity is much cleaner in this respect and offered a much better experience, especially with respect to using the environment as a weapon. With Divinity I felt each power had a time and place, whereas with Pillars I ended up spamming the same powers and hoping for the best.

Story: Pillars of Eternity definity wins out here. While the story in Divinity:OS wasn't bad, I would call it playful to the point of campy. Pillars had a deep, mature fantasy story worthy of a novel. While it was almost too much reading at times, the story was serious, dark, and dealt with real themes. 

Art: Pillars harkens back to the golden age of Infinity Engine games like Balgur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment, etc. The scenes are appealing, but prerendered and they felt a little static. This helps stoke the nostalgia for the late 90s, but Divinity feels up-to-date and immersive. Couple the art style of Divinity with it's highly interactive environments, and the world of Original Sin ends up feeling much more alive. 

Music: Both were great soundtracks but Pillars feels just a bit derivative of the Lord of the Rings movies. They aren't bad at all, but almost generically fantasy at times. Music is important here because when you spend tens of hours in these worlds, you're gonna get this music stuck in your head.

In short, you should play both if you love deep, isometric, high-fantasy, western computer RPGs. If you MUST pick, consider the following choice. Choose Pillars of Eternity if you favor story and choose Divinity: Original Sin if you prefer combat. Both are hallmarks of a great RPG and each specializes beautifully.
I slaughtered the caravan at the very beggining that would usually introduce you into the game, and the story adapted to me bloody evil decision without skipping a beat! Amazing, 10/10!!!

Coming from a background of the early 2010's biggest RPG experiences (Mass Effect 2, Fallout 3, Dark Souls etc.) I came into pillars with some reluctance. It was highly praised, and from a team that had proven chops, but I thought it would be too long, maybe too boring or self-interested, impenetrable or complex for me to navigate properly. I don't dislike fantasy, but having played a lot of WoW and DA growing up, I thought I'd seen it all.

I was wrong, and I was glad I was wrong.

Pillars of Eternity is quite simply a landmark in RPGs. Never have I played a story that treated me as a human being so well, that punished and rewarded my actions with such realism, with characters that are beautiful and troubled and conflicted and who you often do not get to magically save. You engage with them - often, the only way to progess quests is not to fetch some item but to travel with your companions, and learn about why they are the way they are, and maybe help them to see if they could be something else. You listen to their doubts like a dear old friend. You are not always friendly with them - you have real and justified conflict with them if you come from almost any kind of viewpoint. The story refuses, much like New Vegas, to give you easy answers, or to talk your way out of every situation, or to give you a "correct" choice. There are choices that I made in this game that genuinely made me reflect about who I was as a person, and how I treated other people and what I thought was morally sound. You might be the protagonist in this story but you are rarely the Big Hero - you are another person in this complex and complicated world, and you stumble and make mistakes and fail and succeed and that the game can do this without making it feel patently unfair is testimony to narrative design and craft of writing. 

Remember in Fallout:New Vegas, where picking any of the major game endings (spoilers ahead for F:NV here) isn't necessairly the best one? I mean sure, the Legion ending is probably the worst kind of fate overall, but picking the NCR isn't just "the good guys won, now everything's okay" - you come to understand that system's corruption, or the selfishness of Mr.House, or how the independent ending is truely freeing but discards so much praticality for its sake.
Pillars has those kind of choices.

A supreme voice acting cast nails their characters to a T - Eder's dry, blunt manner could be picked straight from my rural town's farming population, to name but one. There isn't  a single character that I dislike, as an experience - Durance is an unmitigated evangelist preacher asshole, and yet as you talk to him you can see why he's like this.

The combat is easily adjustable for how hard you want it, from diehard greybeard brutalist simulations to light affairs between dialog boxes. A rich and rewarding class system means you have all the staples of D&D present, but expanded upon and rarely are their any choices that feel wrong, save outside of very high-level and high-difficulty encounters. You pick a class and you feel like that class - you pick a barbarian, you can dish out appropriately big swings and murderlize everything, but you're not the smartest cookie in the room. It just feels right. Your strategy can be modified as much as you like - wizards can learn an astound variety of spells, and set up crowd control to enable rogues and other hard hitters to quickly end combat, paladins aura buff frontliners to wear down tough enemies - as long as something works, you can really do combat as you like, and you'll get challenges from the game where you must micromanage and work tactically to defeat your foes in battle.

The art, on a direction and technical scale, is impeccable. Not only does it look great, but it does its job as visual storytelling perfectly. The bustling city streets of Defiance Bay, with its many houses, temples, markets, and even a theatre, make it a real place - realer than real. The wilderness locations are beautiful, lush with vegetation or scarred by conflict and neglect, strewn with bones, remind you're not in a safe place anymore. Even small houses creak with age and decay -  you can tell where you are in the world by looking at the interior of a house somewhere, even without knowing anything about the geography of the actual location. All of this is done without becoming overwhelming or confusing. Day and night cycles are represented wonderfully, with lantern-lit streets giving way to poorly-lit roads, or scattered light clusters around smaller towns. The marks of ruin, disasters, the gods and of people is embedded into the game's art masterfully. 

The audio feels right - satisfying clunks and clanks of armor and steel, or the slop of liquid for potions, as you move items around your inventory, the kind of walking sounds I can hear clearly in my head, acidic spells hiss just like real acid, fire spells woomf mightily, divine spells ring with sacred might, pyschic spells radiate alluring energy. The music is tailored to every environment to perfectly complement it - tracks like Oldsong are forever stuck in my head, and the combat music - which you'll hear a lot of- manages to strike the right tone between genuine tension without becoming grating. All of it works, both as standalone pieces of music as well as setting the tone for any zone you care to name.

For the genuine negatives, the base game's Act 3 feels very rushed in parts, and overall the sheer scale of what this game is trying to do clearly was not able to be fully realised -  every game has to cut for time, but there are some things I feel like should've been added - having a much different kind of tone of dialog if you play a priest of Eothas, talking to Eder, is one example. Not all of the game's classes are born equal, and you can often miss out on things on your first time around.

Still, that's a very minor nitpick. This is a triumph of a game, and is one of the few games I unconditionally love. The DLC is not just merely more, but expands to give much more of a wilderness feel- often, you encounter problems that are solved not with wits but with skill and strength, something the base came somewhat neglected in favour of having high intelligence and high lore casters be the real talkers in the game's non-combat situations. There is just so much to see and do and it's all worth it. Buy it.

Ok, PoE2 is on it's way and just recently I decided to finish the game for the second time! I am writing a review now for all those who might have skipped this gem and are considering digging their teeth into PoE1 before the second part comes out. This time I finished the game with The White March expansion and I didn't want to write a review until the whole experience settled. 

First let me just say that there are reviews here who would want you to believe that PoE is vastly inferior to it's spiritual predecessor Baldur's Gate. This is not a problem of course as long as the arguments provided are not objectively false! For example, I can understand someone preferring BG2 to PoE1 due to NPC interactions and romances, since those really are objectively a lot better in BG2! However, when your arguments boil down to: "I love BG2, but PoE sucks because AoE spells damage my allies!"... well... at that point I have to wonder if you even played BG2, since AoE spells always did friendly damage in D&D.

The second thing I want to mention is that all those reviews who say that The White March is just an Icewind Dale style of expansion have no clue what they are talking about! Yes, TWM is set in a snowy part of the world, but that's pretty much the only similarity to Icewind Dale. TWM has a brilliant story of its own, new characters, bunch of new character interactions, multiple ways of solving pretty much every quest in the expansion and bunch of skill checks and choices and consequences that the Icewind Dale series never had! TWM is not a combat focused expansion. It is an expansion that improves and deepens pretty much every aspect of the game with more voice overs, more text adventure parts, more puzzles, more enchanting options, more quests, better quests, deeper lore, etc.

Anyway, if I was to compare PoE1 to BG2, I would say the following. 

Things that BG2 does better:
- NPC banter with playable characters as I already mentioned.
- Romances since PoE doesn't even have any romances.
- Overall general polish is definitely better in BG2. PoE has quite a few minor bugs like the sound suddenly breaking off or sudden framerate drops. These bugs can easily be fixed with a quick reload, but I never had such problems with BG2.
- The biggest problem with PoE are their characters who don't really ever engage into conversations in the same way they did in BG2. Their banter is very short and it usually doesn't lead anywhere. They rarely interject into your conversations with other NPCs and when they do, the other NPCs usually just ignore their interjection. They don't express strong opinions and they rarely or never argue about your choices. As such they are clearly inferior to BG2!
- PoE has some Kickstarter content that is part of the game and which completely breaks immersion. Luckily this is easily noticable and can be avoided, so it's not a big deal - but why did Obsidian even put it into their game is beyond me!
- PoE has no walking option, so this is a real bummer for those of us who like to immerse ourselves into a game. It just looks stupid when you are sprinting in libraries and taverns while everyone else is walking. This is such an easy thing to implement, it boggles my mind why is this not in the game!

Things that PoE1 does better:
- enchanting, cooking and crafting
- text adventure parts which are further expanded on in The White March. In Fact BG2 lacks this feature completely!
- roleplaying flavor in your responses such as "aggressive", "diplomatic", "honest", etc. PoE gives you a lot more flavour here and as such it is far superior to black and white choices of BG2.
- character reputation which effects the dialogue options
- skill checks in dialogues actually allow you to finish certain quests peacfully - something which is a huge problem with BG series, since in BG1 and BG2 pretty much every conversation ends up in violence.
- multiple solutions to puzzles
- different entrances and exists to various quests
- The keep is a lot more developed. You can upgrade it with various useful parts which lead to new quests, powerful equipment, resting buffs, etc. There is the whole mega dungeon to explore there with a whole set of it's own quests.

Things that are a matter of personal preference:
- Combat - Now, I loved combat in BG, but I actually enjoyed combat in PoE more, because PoE doesn't feature any "insta death" spells. This allows the combat to breathe and gives you the opportunity to adjust your strategy depending on what is happening. In BG very often you would just get destroyed in a microsecond and avoiding such death traps would require you to know exactly what each spell does. Even then, there are some insta death spells which you cannot avoid in any way, so you are pretty much at the mercy of a dice roll.
- D&D vs PoE system - I love both, but PoESys is a lot more complicated and difficult to learn. For example in D&D you just have armor class and saving throws to worry about when it comes to your defense. In PoESys you have deflection, damage reduction which comes in 5 different flavours, then there are reflex, fortitude and mental saving throws. Then you have to take into consideration speed reduction and accuracy since armor and shields usually negatively impacts this... so yeah... it can really be hard to understand the whole system, which is probably why a lot of people who like D&D are complaining about it. The upside is that PoESys is a lot more flexible and you can play any type of character you want. People who complain that a wizard has to have high might to be effective are just ignorant and they dont understand the system.
- The story - Both games have a brilliant story and I really can't decide which one I like better, but PoE is darker and delves more deeply into philosophy and human nature, whereas BG feels more like Lord of the Rings.

Conclusion: Both games are masterpieces without a doubt and if you liked BG2 you will also like PoE1! In the end, I would give PoE 9/10 as I would give to BG2. It is a game that every RPG fan should play and support!

If you asked me, "Which game in your library has the most interesting ideas? Asks the most interesting questions? Which game stuck with you long after you finished playing?", PoE would be a top contender. Pillars is a flawed game - a long, meandering title with obvious Kickstarter bloat, and one that frequently touches on real-world issues with all the sensitivity of a sledgehammer - but it is a game with things to say, and I respect it for that.

Above all else, Pillars is an exploration of faith in the context of the D&D-esque fantasy setting. Pillars asks questions like, "What does it mean to have faith in a setting where gods are provable entities with a tangible impact on the world? What does it mean for a god to be 'real'? How can a proven entity be the subject of conflicting interpretation?" These questions are continually reinforced throughout the game - in sidequests, in companions' stories, in the truly excellent White March DLC - in ways that are easier to appreciate in retrospect or on a second playthrough. Pillars' actual narrative may meander, but its themes are a constant, focused presence in a way I really admire. If your favorite part of playing a fantasy RPG is the pantheon and the metaphysics, you owe it to yourself to play this game.

Additionally, I love this game's combat. The greatest praise I can offer is that it makes fighters, of all things, genuinely rewarding to play. There is nothing more satisfying to me than building a couple immovable tanks and using the engagement system to lock up enemies well away from my back line. I also think the combat truly shines on harder difficulties - it's here that the game's excellent buffs and debuffs and its emphasis on tactical positioning rise to the fore. That said, in a game that's already overlong, combat is slow and there's definitely too much of it, so if you find yourself falling off the game, honestly, I recommend putting on story mode and flying through the rest.

I'll say it again: Pillars is a flawed game. My 410 hours of playtime reflect several successful playthroughs, but also many, many failed playthroughs where I fell off the game halfway or even 3/4ths of the way through, forgot where I was in the plot, and started over just to fall off again. And yet I kept *wanting* to come back to this game, and I found it rewarding to replay. I'm glad to have seen it through to its end, and I'm excited to see what the sequel holds.

Oh boi, let's begin!

Pillars of Eternity is a smartly-designed role-playing masterpiece which alongside second part is the best game Obsidian has ever made. It is, essentially, a throwback to older computer roleplaying games. Upon starting up the game you will choose your race, background and class before embarking on an epic quest. The character starts off in the middle of a trip to an area called the Dyrwood. A promise to start a new life in the town of Gilded Vale. Things quickly go tits up and before long you’re scrambling to stay alive. From here things only manage to get worse. You’re dragged into a conflict that will take you across the length and breadth of the Dyrwood as you attempt to uncover an ancient conspiracy and its effects on the land. You’ll see both the good, the bad and the ugly sides of this beautiful, horrifying land. Battles will range from minor skirmishes with bandits and animals to tough brawls with ancient monstrosities.

Pillars of Eternity doesn’t skimp on letting you customize how you experience this conflict. You pick from one of six races, each with between two and four sub-race options. Then you get to pick your class from one of eleven, some of these also having sub-choices to make. Lastly, you’ll have your culture and background – your culture provides starting equipment based on your class while your background provides you with small skill boosts. When you’re done with this your character is truly your own. Even as you pick up NPC allies you’ll often find that they have wildly different choices to yourself so even if you picked the same race / class combo they still feel different.

The game rewards careful wordplay, unlocking alternative quest paths or entirely new situations if you pick your phrasing with foresight. The reputation you cultivate through your responses will come back to you, often, and even make certain statements available to you. As an example, my character developed a reputation for blunt honesty, and as a result, there were several scenarios in which my word alone served as enough proof for certain characters. The reputation system is subtle, but it lends a sense of believable to the niche you carve for your protagonist, and makes it that much easier to get invested in your role. Aside from creating numerous interesting happenings to get yourself involved in, Obsidian also rewards those who dig around before making a quick decision. You might find evidence to contradict a liar, hear the other side of a story that seems cut-and-dry, or come across something that allows you to please both parties in a conflict. This kind of game design allows for you to feel as though you have a much greater impact on the world that just the slash of your sword or the cut of your tongue, and pulls you in that much more effectively.

But what if your role-playing fantasy involves you, 20 Might, and a very big hammer? Pillars does an equally great job of allowing you to live out your dream of being a burly, smash-first-ask-questions-never type, giving a variety of conversation and quest options built around your strength, physique, and intimidation factor. Of course, if you prefer letting your favorite implement of whacking do the talking, Pillars has a wonderful party-based combat system to let you do so. If you’ve played the games upon which Pillars is modeled, you’ll know the basics. Your team of six adventurers can be given commands as a group or individually during the real-time combat, though you have the option of pausing at any time (and can set many conditions for the game to auto-pause for you, if you choose) to assess the battlefield. Much as tabletop Dungeons & Dragons has done in recent years, Obsidian has intelligently made many skills have finite uses per battle, rather than per rest (though the latter still exists). This means your mages and druids will have more to do than lurk in the corner and hope they don’t get one-shotted in each battle. In fact, with every class now given a robust selection of talents, traits, and spells to work with, each melee has an extra layer of strategy. Your heavy-hitters can engage several targets to keep them from attacking over your squishier pals, and managing the various buffs, curses, stuns, and spells between your party means every fight is quite interesting. 

Class-building is also rather free-form. Each character has specific class abilities and a role in combat, but the nature of the armor system– that is, that anyone can wear any piece of gear– along with perk specializations means that you can have that heavy armor-wearing battle mage you always dreamed of. Donning weightier equipment slows your character’s action recovery speed, though, so you won’t be striking or spellcasting quite as fast as a less-encumbered companion. Skill choices have a sense of weight, because they define who your character will become; with a level cap of 16, you’re encouraged to make choices about your party’s growth that will absolutely affect how you approach combat throughout the game.

The interface and systems guiding all of this is are rather good ones, and it makes managing the party’s inventory and battle inventory quite simple. Crafting, comparing, and equipping all take relatively few clicks to work with, and the ability to minimize most of the UI during exploration is a welcome chance from the omnipresent frame walling in past Infinity Engine adventures. Character pathfinding across long distance is generally quite good, although you will have to manage who walks where during encounters in tight spaces, as your ranged fighters do tend to enjoy blocking your melee machines from getting to the action. The addition of slow and fast-motion speeds was also an excellent choice, as the former allows you to bypass battle pausing if you’re so inclined, and the latter allows you to quickly retread ground you’ve covered numerous times already.

While the game isn’t going to set your graphics card on fire (arguably a good thing), it’s still detailed and full of polish and beauty. The environments to tend towards the dank and dingy of European fantasy, and many of them are variations of “forest, cave, dungeon,” but there’s still a surprising amount of variety between those archetypes. Character models look rather good (though their diminutive size does make it hard to see at times), and the various suits of armor and weapons all have an effect on their in-game appearance. Spells in particular look awesome, with all kinds of lights and particle effects dancing across the screen. The music is all excellent, following in the tradition of Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale.

Summing up Pillars of Eternity is a dense, lengthy, fascinating adventure that you will remember for a long time.

Baldur's Gate 1, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights, this game follows in those kinds of footsteps. I think alot of folks made the mistake of comparing this game to the best of the genre, Baldur's Gate 2, and to a lesser extent Planescape Torment.

So, what are you getting with this game? For those NOT born in the golden era of the CRPG, this game is basically a pausable real time strategy game with HEAVY character building, party management, loot, and good old fashioned dungeon crawling in between beautiful overworld map exploration. You build a party of heroes and follow a story line to explore a fantasy world. You level up your character in a similar fashion to table top roleplaying games, which means you can make whatever you want. Few games afford the in depth systems that allow you to create any character you can imagine, we are talking MMO level customization here. As an example, my first ever character was a 2 handed human barbarian. My most recent was a bow-wielding ranger who has a fairly upgraded wolf companion. Add in the rest of the party and you can customize and min-max to your hearts content.

Companions come in your typical story companions, or you can make your own and further min-max your favorite party composition. I prefer the story companions. Much like Dragon's Age or Baldurs gate, your companions react to you, and each have distinct personalities, and will offer their thoughts from time to time or a quest. Now, this is an Obsidian game. Which means you have a whole different style of writing than your typical Bioware or Bethesda RPG. The problem here is that your traveling companions are less stereotypical than something like Dragon Age. These people feel much more real, and frankly, this makes them for the most part, alot less interesting than companions in other games. Stick with it, and you will find that Obsidian did a good job. You certainly won't like all of them, but they fit the world rather well.

Speaking of, the world's environments are stark, brutal, and downright gorgeous. This isn't your typical DnD type fantasy. Rolling green fields don't make up 90% of the game like Baldurs gate. Hell, I'd compare it more readily to Path of Exile's Wraeclast. My second favorite aspect of these types of games are exploring each 'area' on the map. Really feels like you are traveling the lands of a fantasy world.

The overall lore for the setting is great. The overall story? ...not so much. Obsidian has real trouble with keeping the player engaged. I have something like 150 hours in Fallout New Vegas, and I've never finished it. Obsidian just doesn't make the player feel involved very well. Honestly the story strikes me ALOT like Kingdoms of Amalur. You have a special power, and instead of influencing fate like that title, you can see peoples past lives and affect their souls. A mysterious robed figure may or may not be involved. You see where this is going. I used to think Dragon's Age's Darkspawn where some of the lamest plot hook bad guys ever created..... than I came upon PoE. Listen, this game hearkens back to Baldurs Gate 1, where you kind of just wandered around aimlessly with the attitude of 'lets go on an adventure'. Same thing applies here. If you need a cohesive focused story, you will not like this game. The main story just sort of unfolds around you over time. Its supposed to feel more realistic and dynamic. In the end however, you will end up forgetting all about it for a large portion of the game. Exploration is really a key part of this title...

...which leads to difficulty. The game doesn't scale enemies, and is extremely bad at letting you know you just wandered into an area which you can't ever hope to beat. You might think that after the tutorial a bear is an easy fight... you would be wrong. Combat plays out like DnD or an MMO raid. You need frontliners, damage dealers, healers, and crowd control. Combat is EXTREMELY involved. You should be micromanaging your party, and activating abilities, using equipment, and generally trying not to die. The mechanics are fairly advanced, and you will need to spend time learning the mechanics before you take on the real threats. Unlike Baldur's Gate 2, spellcasters aren't the do all end all of the game. It doesn't devolve into a card game where each spell is used to counter another in epic magical duals... but you still need to learn all the spells, figure out which ones will be most useful for the upcoming encounter, and you should be buffing the living crap out of your party. There is ALOT going on combat wise, and after exploration, combat should be on your mind at all times.

Pillars of Eternity is a game that really harkens back to the 90's era crpg. This isn't a casual game, and if you don't have experience with the genre, its a good starting point. Unlike the older titles it eases you in with a good tutorial, and nice graphics. It also isn't nearly as difficult as BG2. (or the end of BG1 for that matter. I had no shame cheesing the last boss.) If you do have experience with these types of games, its absolutely worth it. It may not be BG2, but it offers a new take on the genre, which I think holds up extremely well. Now if you will excuse me, I have to clear this dungeon so I can get another level and spend 30 minutes agonizing over the best perk to choose.

Baldur's Gate was the ultimate videogame for me when I was a kid, but I've always had trouble convincing my friends to like it. The same is true now for Pillars of Eternity. The quality of the game is super, it's just an inaccessible format to some people.  I think this is probably the game for you if you can enjoy a fantasy novel or have ever read up on the lore of a videogame outside of the game. 

The thing this type of game does best is world building. The characters you meet have weight, everything matters, and the universe feels unique. It's not a cheap knockoff fantasy world where they just switch around the names of familiar tropes. There's a holistic personality to the world you're in and you just want to get to know it. And the best part is that getting to know the world doesn't mean reading through the codexes in a menu somewhere. The game teases bits of lore and it's up to you to find out more. You learn about a war and you have to meet a veteran to find out what happened. You find the name of a god and you seek out a priest to learn their beliefs. You'll hear someone tell a myth and you'll actually seek out the book in game so you can get the full story. And even then, no one source is definitive, so you're delighted if you ever stumble upon a new tidbit.

Pillars Of Eternity is a story-rich isometric fantasy R.P.G. developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Paradox Interactive. You take on the role of an adventurer hoping to start a new life for yourself by making your way towards Gilded Vale where there's a promise of land to be given and riches to be made. As the caravan that you're traveling with makes camp for the night it's suddenly besieged upon by hostile warriors and through a series of unfortunate events you soon find yourself gifted with the abilities of a "Watcher". This strange power allows you to see into the souls, memories and past lives of individual people. How does one control this power? How do they use it? How do I get rid of it? Prepare to go on an expansive journey through a rich fantasy setting as you seek answers for this affliction that you've suddenly found yourself burdened with. Is the power of a "Watcher" a glorious gift or a terrible curse...only time will tell?

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

The bread and butter of most great roleplaying games is the opportunity to create your own character and in this aspect Pillars Of Eternity excels. The character customization here is quite detailed offering you a variety of different races to choose from as well as a plethora of skills, character classes and backstories to select. Not to mention the huge gallery of gorgeous handpainted profile images that you can pick from for your hardy adventurer. In typical R.P.G. fashion your characters earn experience points as they complete quests, various tasks or defeat enemies which then allow you to level up thus granting access to a number of skill points. These points can then be applied to an abundance of abilities to further enhance your group in anyway that you see fit. There's also a wide array of weapons, armor and trinkets available for you to purchase, loot or craft as you adventure. Over the course of the game you will also encounter a number of scripted events that you'll have to deal with based on the skills, knowledge and equipment that your group possesses. I found these encounters to be quite intriguing and just alot of fun. I'm only guessing but I assume that the scripted events also pay hommage to the old "pen and paper" R.P.G.'s from back in the day? 

Combat is party-based and real time. You have the option to set each of your party members "A.I." or you can choose to turn that off and micromanage each person's actions in battle which is what I prefer to do. There's a pause function which you can use to stop and start combat so you can issue orders on the fly as well as observe every single action that takes place during a battle. The combat is extremely addictive and quite challenging just as it should be. Yet another aspect of the game is that you will gain access to your very own stronghold that you'll be able to restore as you see fit which I also found to be really interesting. It's not cheap and it takes time but returning to your keep and seeing the progress that's being made on it's restoration is quite pleasing not to mention the myriad of bonuses, situations and people that the stronghold attracts. Add to that the huge amount of intriguing quests that you will go on over the progression of this title and the gameplay increases significantly. In summary, Pillars Of Eternity does an exceptional job of immersing you in a brilliantly conceived fantasy world with rich lore, excellent gameplay and fantastic combat.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

As an isometric title you won't find many more that can top the visuals in Pillars Of Eternity. I love to play these types of games with the camera zoomed all the way out as I find they tend to look their best like this but that's just my personal opinion. With that said, beautiful lighting and immersive weather patterns really help to bring life to the varied locations. This title looks truly amazing with crisp textures, a vast color palette and lots of nicely detailed set pieces that really flush out the top-down isometric environments whether you're casually walking around a bustling city or nervously trudging through a monster infested dungeon. Likewise, the game stays true to it's setting with the abundant amount of fantasy inspired locations that you visit as your adventures take you across the land of Eora. Quaint villages, huge fortresses, bustling medieval cities and forested regions laden with wild animals and highwaymen looking to pilfer your coin. Also, the aural presentation is just as robust with excellent sound effects and a absolutely amazing orchestral soundtrack. In short, the developers managed quite well to put forth a truely immersive presentation for this fascinating R.P.G. title.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

Experiencing this game took me back to the nostalgic days of playing "Baldur's Gate" which is without a doubt one of the all-time best R.P.G.'s ever. With that said, I thoroughly enjoyed Pillars Of Eternity with it's fascinating lore, gripping narrative and of course the addictive party-based real-time combat. This game truly harkens back to a time when the isometric R.P.G. ruled the gaming world and what a glorious time that it was. As options go, there are many Steam Achievements to hunt down and Steam Trading Cards to collect. D.L.C. is available in the form of "The Deadfire Pack", "The White March Part I", "The White March Part II" and a number of other items ranging from ringtones to wallpapers as well as a superb original soundtrack laden with twenty six wonderfully orchestrated songs. In conclusion, if you're looking to go on an exhilarating adventure through a very impressive fantasy world filled with interesting mythology, memorable characters and challenging combat then Pillars Of Eternity is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to R.P.G., story-rich, adventure and isometric gamers one and all!!!

This is one of those games where the more you play, the less you like it. I was all pumped when I first got it, and as you can see I have put a lot of hours into it. I l-o-v-e games like Baldurs Gate, Icewind dale and early Fallout. But you start to notice things in this game which makes no sense, and then these issues grow, and when I go to play it now, everything seems completely irrational.

Might controls your physical prowess, and your magic prowess. I can accept that, but it also means that my wizard is fully capable of lifting a human being over his head. Like... Que? And I don't mean I could theoretically do that. It's in the actual game. Because you have a high might score, you can lift someone above your head even though you're playing a skinny human. I guess all mages are also weight lifters in Pillars of Eternity?

Going barbarian seems awesome, right? Who doesn't like Conan? But you imagine barbarians as large and strong and perhaps not as intellectual. Nuh-uh, not in Pillars of Eternity. The best stat to increase as a barbarian is intelligence, because that controls your AOE swings with your weapon. Second best would be perception, because you kinda need those swings to hit. Third best is might.

Might is third??? But this is a berserking barbarian!
"Yep, we think berserking is controlled by intelligence" <--- POE reasoning.

Like... Wha? So barbarians are generally super smart and really observant of their surroundings, but wizards are generally bulky? I mean, if you're going with what's good stat wise.

And then there's the "combat only" spells. Like, you have a fireball and you want to start the fight with that? Can't be done. You have to first start the fight somehow. Apparently, deciding to throw a fireball at someone cannot be done before you first throw a rock at them or exchange harsh words. I mean even if you did decide to make some sort of warrior-wizard or something, you know - synergy since might controls both physical strength and spell power, that wizard can't buff himself pre combat. Can't be done. Impossible. He knows no spells before he gets angry. Wizards are like some sort of dysfunctional versions of Hulk.

"Oh you don't want to get me mad, because then... Then I will suddenly know arcane knowledge. Not before! No. But after. Grr."

And then there's the resting issue. You buy camping gear at inns and shops, but there's a limited supply. Like... Wait. I can rent a room here, and eat here, and drink here, but I can't take food or gear with me? In this game, you have an unlimited inventory. It's unlimited, aside camping gear. I can literally bring with me a gazillion swords, but I can't pack a tent, some wood, some food and something too drink. I can outfit 6000 legions through my inventory. But some bread and a flask of water? Noooo... Can only have... 4.. of those. For some reason.

These things just go on and on and on and I want to play this game again. I do. But I can't. It's just... I... I'm just not high enough. I don't have enough brain damage to find these things reasonable.

I recommend this game to people who are mostly interested in optimizing builds, but no one else. Because it's really fun tinkering around with what can be done with different builds and whatnot. But if you're after an engaging story and just... Things that make sense somehow. No. No amount of fan boy fawning can save this mechanic.

First off, I'm gonna start with some beginner tips because omg I wish these were explained through the tutorial:

* Press "tab" to highlight intractable objects - I spent the first half of the game not knowing about this and OMG was it annoying. I thought "shift" would highlight interactable objects initially because this is the key I'm most familiar with using in CRPGs. 
* Set your controls to change the camera movement settings from arrow keys to W, A, S, and D. This helps a lot. 
* Make sure to mess around with the customizable formation tabs. Some formations may cause your characters to get stuck in doorways, which is a hassle to fix, so make sure to set up a "filing" formation and switch between formations before entering a doorway. 
* Do not explore a location unless its either a location you'll regularly visit (ex. a tavern or inn which you'll likely need to frequent). Otherwise, you'll waste time. Only explore the location once you receive the quest related to said location. 
* Do not feel bad or ashamed for looking things up. Trust me, I had to look up locations and major NPC locations far more than once. I highly recommend playing story mode first just so you can figure out quest objectives/locations. The game goes by MUCH faster once you know. 
* Storywise, I recommend playing Cipher because Cipher gets a lot of story content. The best way to play Cipher, however, is a major glass canon build, which can be hard for beginners to figure out. Melee Cipher is possible, but arguably less effective. I know storywise, none of the backgrounds and locations of origin have much content in POE1, but archipelgo islands and aristocrat backgrounds have much more content is POE2 if you plan on importing a POE1 save to POE2. 
* Make sure to set up your character properly stat and class-wise because you will not be able to make changes mid-game. Look up a guide if you're unsure of yourself. 
* You can change your party at any tavern. Just look for the party tab. You can change your skills (not stats/class) at any vendor. 

I honestly feel like my standards have gotten too high because of BG3. But here are my personal pros and cons. 

Cons: 
* I wish there was more actual "roleplaying" involved. I feel like my character's background was hardly mentioned and the dialogue options struck me as "super good", "stoic/neutral", or "super evil" only. Overall, MC shapes the world around them, but the world around them does not really shape the MC. 
* Sometimes background specific dialogue gets locked or not mentioned because of choices you made far earlier in the game, which is disappointing to see. (ex. I let the noble girl get possessed by the Skaenite slaves in Act 1, as RP wise my character had a slave background and just wanted to see nobles burn, but where Skaen is supposed to mention the MC's slave background to both MC and the party in Act 3, he doesn't and instead remarks how impressive the MC's actions during this event were.) I think it can still be assumed/headcannoned that your party knows about your character's background, but there's no reaction to it. This is the same case with POE2. It'd be cool if party members questioned my evil actions during this event, because most party members are good/neutral characters, and I could then explain my disdain for nobles due to my MC's slave background. Overall, the actual "roleplay" aspect of the series is kinda weak. 
* Why do major NPCs look like minor NPCs? More than once, I found it difficult to locate major NPCs because they looked so damn average. Meanwhile, some unimportant NPCs LOOK like they should be major NPCs which pisses me off. 
* There are still some bugs with gameplay. 
* I feel like the companions could've used longer questlines--especially the companions you encounter at the very beginning of the game. I was actually disappointed with how short Eder and Aloth's quests were. The good thing is that most companion quests follow the MC's main questline, so you can travel to wherever you need to go along the way. 
* AI gets confused pretty often. Especially in doorways. It's better to just turn it off and manually control characters for every move, but at the same time it gets hectic, so I avoided doing this unless the battle was a major battle. 
* It's difficult to find certain locations. Many times, I had to look up where to go. Sometimes graphical glitches actually obscured or outright didn't allow me to get to where I needed to go. (Ex. at the final Shadow dungeon (forgot its name) a shadow continued to obscure the stairway I needed to go down to get to Thaos. I had to look up where to go, and I realized this. The stairway only revealed itself after I reloaded the dungeon.)
* Holy F*** the amount of time I spent staring at loading screens probably made up at least 25% of my playthrough. I feel like one thing Obsidian gets wrong that Larian figured out is that each act should be set in one location with few loading required locations. Otherwise, there is far too much back and forth.
* At least 50% of the game is walking from location to location. I think pillars of eternity 2 actually fixes this by condensing the maps slightly. 
* Caed Nua restoration is neat, but I feel like it was underwhelming with the lack of content. I was hoping to see storylines/quests unlock as a result of fixing parts of Caed Nua. (Maybe I missed these? Idk) 
* You, unfortunately, can't change your stats/build/class mid-game. You can only change your skills. 

Pros: 
* Matt Mercer's voice. No, I totally did not just side with the evil Skaenite Wymgourd because he was also voiced by Matt Mercer. 
* Gameplay is fun once you figure it out. I honestly restarted my game 3 times to figure it out. 
* A lot of world building. Arguably, sometimes too much. I did forget major names/titles/events very often as I explored. 
* A lot of gameplay build options
* A lot of reading for reading lovers such as myself. 
* Replayability. There are a lot of builds to mess around with, and there are different choices you can make to impact the ending. 
* Although there is a limited number of choices, they do still impact the storyline. I'm just disappointed they're not as prominent once imported to POE2. 
* Most of the companions are interesting and likeable. My favorite was Eder not just because of his voice, his role in POE2 and his close relationship with the MC, but because he was a major meatshield for my glass cannon Cipher build lol. Eder is a total bro (sadly just a bro). I think you'll like him even more in POE2. 

Overall, the game is enjoyable, but I think I'll be focusing more on POE2 because I think it fixes a lot of issues of POE1. Again, I still feel like Obsidian doesn't understand the most optimal CRPG formula like Larian does because both POE1/2 can get really frustrating at times. Sometimes, I was so frustrated I considered quitting, but i'm glad I made it all the way through. I think POE1 is a one and done game for me though.

First of all, YES it is a good game and I'd recommend to anyone looking for a CRPG as a newcomer to the genre.

BUT, I have several points to make about the game, the biggest one has already been solved in PoE2.

- Real time combat system: it is not really useful. It is nice while you have 1-3 party members, but as soon as you have a mage, a priest, and then a full 6-member party the micromanagement gets so thick that the game ends up being turn based anyway. You pause, issue commands, unpause, see combat for a second, pause again to issue new commands.

- This is something that affects two CRPGs I've already played (Disco Elysium, Divinity OS E): the quests are so cryptically written that, without a guide, you end up stumbling upon dozens of other quests not knowing where to go, not even having a single clue. Once you look information up on the internet, you are able to quickly solve quests but the point is that most of them should be more streamlined and devs could abandon this whole "you can go anywhere!" marketing selling point because it doesn't quite work. Make it more streamlined, make it so you can focus on important quests only, save time not writing so many minor quests/tasks that add nothing to the experience. This is a point that damages other genres as well but in a long CRPG such as PoE it gets very hard to endure misplaced quests later in the game that reward you with laughable XP, worthless items and zero lore or world-building.

- The difficulty: "story mode" is too easy, the following difficulty level is too hard (for anyone that plays as a pastime and not as a full-time job), and I can't imagine how hard the other levels are. The way monsters are distributed on the map without a logic level progression, in which sometimes you find bosses or mobs incredibly difficult but then the rest of the area is super easy, or the way the whole last area is super easy but then the last boss is unbearably difficult. I know I could've gotten a couple more levels, but the game could have given me this hint 8 hours earlier making these last areas and tasks harder and demanding me to acquire more levels/gear.

Again, this is my personal opinion and everyone will have different experiences. I bought the game mainly to support the devs and to better understand the lore of the second game, but you can straight up jump to the second game in the series and have a better experience.

TLDR: [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] suffers from a fanservice-induced identity crisis and is an unengaging RPG.

Okay...
I made four approaches to this game - somewhere from 15 to 50 hours each.
I never got around to finishing it, and I clearly never will.
Now I can safely say that I don't like [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] and don't recommend it as an RPG.
Yes, I'm that much of an idiot to spend so much time determining that fact.
But it's because I tried to like this game. I hoped to find merit to it.
I cannot say I didn't, but it wasn't nearly enough.

Just to give some context: I'm younger than the demographic that played [i]Baldur's Gate[/i] on its release - granted. But the charm of this type of RPG isn't lost on me - I had a wonderful time with [i]Neverwinter Nights 2[/i], and especially with [i]Mask of the Betrayer[/i]. I also liked [i]Dragon Age[/i], the first. And I played  classics later. So, it's not the real-time-with-pause that repels me although I have to admit - managing a six-man squad with as many filler encounters as this game has is fiddly at best and exhausting at worst.

[i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] could be very good potentially - it tries to be calm and collected while not shying away from unnerving themes. It has very little pomp and should be commended for it.

[b]But it has no focus. Just none.[/b]

What is [i]Baldur's Gate[/i] about? We can all answer easily: it's about the legacy of the protagonist (story-wise) and the joy of adventure (impression-wise).
What is [i]Planescape: Torment[/i] about? The recollection of self (story-wise) and the discovery of a strange world (impression-wise).
What are the first [i]Fallouts[/i] about? It's about saving your people (story-wise) and surviving the harsh and bleak world (impression-wise).
What is [i]Dragon Age[/i] about? Stemming the tide of horrors - both story-wise and impression-wise.

What on God's green Earth is [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] about? Hm? Story-wise it's about the calm and horrible pandemic of soulless babies being born, and about the circulation of soul, and about the deicide that is connected to this pandemic, and the protagonist is a Watcher who sees straight into the soul, and we should find  what causes it. And then there's this ancient machinery that deals in soul stuff. And the strange magical winds that threaten the soul too. And the eponymous pillars of adra stone through which soul circulates. And I have to piece it all together? Alright. So, it's a detective game? With a mystery at its center. Except literally everything else is distracting me from solving it.

I can run errands.
I can run filler errands.
Then more errands.
And then some more.
I can build my own castle. Why?! What purpose does it serve? I mean, I understand it thematically: I claimed it, I'm moving up in the world, but it doesn't serve any plot purpose. You may never touch it again after claiming it - and it will be fine with the game.
I can descend into a long dungeon crawl under my castle, because something horrible dwells in there that might challenge my ownership. But it's again unrelated to the main plot and the game won't mind if I ignore it.
I can investigate rumors about an entirely different matter if I bought the DLC.

So, it's a game about side-content first and foremost? Adventure. Then why such mysterious and bleak main plot? It's not an epic adventure [i]Baldur's Gate[/i]-style. It tries to induce dread and hopelessness. Until the next errand.

[b][i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] has very poor pacing[/b]. 
So, I did my fair share of weald-scourging, went into dungeons under my castle, now it's time for the big city. Huzzah! I eagerl go in there: finally, a change of pace, factions, sewers, quarters, taverns, street gangs... The city is explored, its plotline complete, the tension racks up, we set out into the countryside again, and I will soon catch up with the mysterious man again... And then the second city strikes! No more vodka, I'm drunk enough! That's where I quit the game three out of four times, and the fourth time I didn't make it much further than that. Why is that city there? It obliterates all momentum the story could retain!

[b]Companions[/b]
There can be personal preferences, of course, but the only genuinely well-written one is Eder. He's ambiguous, he plays a nice low-key humorous stoic guy, but inside he's broken and doubtful and a bit spiteful, and at the same time he's not an intellectual self-diver keen on introspection. He feels like a human, and he is the only thing I unconditionally enjoyed here.
The rest of the cast are stereotypes. More original stereotypes than in most games, but stereotypes nonetheless.

And there's no pace to companions too! Some you may encounter some 20-30 hours into the game. Why? Why so late? I already have a well-established party!

[b][i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] in very even. No contrast.[/b] Imagine a music graph. There are ups and downs in the melody. If this game were a melody - it would be a barren plain. There are so few distinctive moments to be had for some reason. There are companion questlines, but they somehow fall short. There are sidequests, but they mostly consist of killing things and lack satisfying resolution. There is faction rivaly, but what's so special about these factions? There's our castle, but why is it there? There's even a court hearing like in [i]Neverwinter Nights 2[/i], but it feels so unneccessary.

And the converstaions are so strerile! There's so little I can say, no matter what kind of character I am. And the principle 'press skill-related phrase to win' applies except in the tutorial sequence.

I have so many questions: why? why? why?
And the answer is simple.
Kickstarter.
To attract the audience, [i]Obsidian[/i] promised to bring party-favorites to the table. There was castle-management in [i]Neverwinter Nights 2[/i], so let's have one! There was an optional dungeon of huge proportions in every of the classical D&D RPG - even [i]Planescape: Torment[/i] had its cube! So let's have it! There were six companions in [i]Baldur's Gate[/i], so let's have six too! And that second city? I read interviews. People in [i]Obsidian[/i] understood that many players would come to that second city exhausted, but - well! - promises made on Kickstarter are to be honored! As if it provided the main bulk of funding or anything... Just so you know - [i]Obsidian[/i] got back up  from its knees not because of Kickstarter or even the success of [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] for that matter, but thanks to their very own [i]World of Tanks[/i] clone - [i]Armored Warfare[/i].

So why would this game be focused? Why would conversations be characteristic? Why would the plot be impactful? It's a mishmash of everything. Not without rhyme or reason, granted, but [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] exists not to tell a story, not to give role-playing opportunities, not to immerse a player - no, it exists to be a nostalgic collage.

PS
Buy it only if you're a huuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuge fan of real-time-with-pause gameplay.

PPS
If you really want to try something like this, just play [i]Tyranny[/i] instead. It has all the focus in the world, isn't weighed down by CRPG-fan-appeasing and has compelling writing.

One of the few steam reviews I've written, but this game does so much right and does a few major things wrong that just make it really miserable to play. I've played Baldur's Gate and all the classics that this game attempts to follow and I'm about 30 hours in and have not completed it yet. It's a solid game with lots of value, but there will be points that make you just want to rip your hair out.

[b]AI/Path finding[/b] - Garbage. Your team mates are completely useless and will often get themselves killed if you let the AI control them. You instead have to micro manage EVERY LITTLE ENCOUNTER like crazy to avoid getting screwed. It starts to feel more like baby sitting suicidal dodo's than leading a band of adventurers.

[b]Difficulty scaling[/b] - You can go from breezing through an area to a random fight with no real pretense where you just get embarassingly shut down. Comes out of no where and you just feel cheated. If it was built up or presented as a boss fight or something sure, but the randomness of difficult encounters is frustrating. Fights are either way too easy or way too hard. Very rarely is there an in between. Sometimes there's a trick you need for the fight, but it's not like the game eases you into it or hints that it'll be a special fight so you'll just get spanked by a random group of trash mobs until you catch on and then it'll go back to being a cake walk. It's not exactly awful, but it just leaves you scratching your head and asking where the heck did that come from quite a bit.

[b]Engagement/Aggro system[/b] - Dumb, confusing, and frustrating. Enemies will just magically stick to some characters based on god knows what. Once something is stuck, it's a headache to unstick. Sometimes there is just a stupid amount of enemies and it's impossible to protect your back line in some fights. Not sure what the developers were thinking when the enemy out numbers you 2 : 1 and you only have probably 2 tanks. This situation combined with the 2 items listed above just make me alt f4 at times and come back later because you just feel so cheated by the game.

This game has some very rabid fans. Any criticisms regardless of how accurate they might be will get torn apart and the community just says git gud. This game is very very good at telling a story, but there is no denying that it has some serious gameplay flaws. I would definitely grab it for $25 or less, but only pay more if you can swallow some frustration and really enjoy an emersive, story telling, old school RPG.

After playing the Diablo, Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Icewind Dale, Dragon Age and Divinity Original Sin series i came across this gem of a game. I was hoping it would resemble any of the enumerated games and i guess it was a mix of them, give or take a few aspects.

The Good:
- Superb main story and side content
- Deep characters with personal quests
- A world very rich in lore, very easy to get lost reading and listening to stories about it
- Graphics and Music
- Races and sub-races
- interesting classes
- The diversity of items
- Infinite inventory space (no inventory management required, just pick everything up)
- Choice matters
- Excellent expansion

The Bad:
- Loading screens are too long and too many
- Health vs Endurance system is confusing at first
- Game is difficult in the beginning if you are playing for the first time
- Max level 16. I reached max level at the start of Act 3 so any experience gathered beyond that was pointless
- A bug prevented me from completing one of my companion's personal quest

Advice:
- Pick up everything
- Try to gather a full party as soon as you can
- Don't do the dungeon in Gilded Vale (the first town) until you have a fully functional party, with tank and healer
- Don't rush quests, Take your time and remember this game is not hack and slash
- Always carry with you the following tools: Rope and grappling hook, prybar, hammer and chisel, lockpicks and camping supplies
- Don't hesitate to backtrack to inns for resting if you are out of camping supplies
- Make sure to always have a character with high mechanics skill
- The game really picks up once you get your keep
- Once you build the Warden's Lodge in the keep, go inside and the NPC will give you bounty quests worth lots of exp and good items
- Once you get legendary items (silver color), make sure to bind them to the character they are equipped on and do the mini-quests written on them to access bonus properties on them
- Enchant your items
