[h2]Pillars Of Eternity Definitive Edition Review[/h2]

I never intended to spend much time on this game; probably 40-50 hrs at most, but before I knew it I had ended up spending 120+ hours in-game! Review is after completing the main game and all dlc and both expansions; including all main quests, companion quests, side quests and tasks on Normal difficulty. 

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
[list]
[*]I enjoyed all the reading, especially the named NPC backstories. All the expertly written exposition surprisingly helped with one of my English exams!

[*]The game allowed me to delay levelling up, which is a highly appreciated feature. I was able to level up based on the challenge the game offered at each progressive stage.

[*]The game had a relaxed inventory system that promoted hoovering up all loot. After all, in a world with magic why would they even need to worry about carry-weight?

[*]I particularly liked the Wizards summoning of [b]thick[/b] [i]slimy[/i] tentacles with which to pound enemies!

[*]The game soundtrack was entertaining and the option to download it and enjoy it at leisure was most welcome.

[*]Side quests supplied choices that had both large and small consequences in later Acts and in the ending.

[*]This game is called the spiritual successor to Baldur’s Gate; in my opinion this is appropriate.

[*]Companion quests had strong writing, excellent voice acting and were quite varied. I liked how some of them provided closure while others didn’t necessarily do so; as is often the case in reality.

[*]There are no romance options in the game. Perfect! It would have made zero sense for my wild Orlan to romance my odd brigade of companions. Obsidian didn’t shoehorn romance into this game and that is ideal.

[*]Figuring out the use of AI combat patterns and group formations felt smooth and organic.

[*]At the beginning of the DLC and Act3, the game inquired if I wanted to increase the challenge as I was overleveled. I declined, as the overleveled state was intentional. But the feature to ask the player’s choice was most welcome.

[*]The game provides named unique items, which can be upgraded or enchanted depending on the item type. The DLC also adds more unique weapons that can be bound to certain characters by fulfilling various conditions. I felt this was a very thematic and appropriate system considering the lore of the game.

[*]I was quite saturated at the point of playing the White March Part 2. Over 100 hours in this game I never intended to invest in. So I lowered the difficulty a notch to help speed through fights faster. As such, the ability to adjust difficulty at any time was much appreciated.

[*]Notable voice acting by the actors for Eder, Aloth and Durance. All other companions also have superb voice acting. Moreover, I felt the main villain’s voice actor played their part incredibly well. The majority of side characters also had decent voice acting.

[*]Speaking of world building: now that I have devoted over 100+ hours into this game I am fully invested in the world of Eora. All that’s left to say is: “More please!”

[*]The game dropped hints of the Deadfire Archipelago, setting up some lore for the next game.
[/list]
[h3]Cons:[/h3]
[list]
[*]While it appeared enticing to obtain all the achievements of this game, some of them required a level of dedication I simply couldn’t spare.

[*]At the 90% mark of Act 2, I felt overloaded. After exploring the entire world map thus far, the game dumped a new capital city with its own culture and lore on me. I was weighed down by this, especially because I felt their culture was uncivilised and barbaric and it tested my patience. Perhaps because, at this point I just wanted to be done with Act 2.

[*]Loading times were bad right from the beginning of the game and progressively got worse. Quicksaving felt like the easier option. Manual saving or loading felt like a painful option.

[*]When playing the White March Part 2 I experienced occasional freezing of the game. Waiting for about 1 to 2 minutes resolved these issues.

[*]When loading the save file list doing a mouse click would freeze the game. Windows asked whether to close POE but being patient resolved the issue.
[/list]
[h3]Advice:[/h3]
[list]
[*]I played while occasionally referring to a walkthrough from Gamefaqs. I learned that lesson from playing Divinity Original Sin. My advice is explore and play a new map area/dungeon as you please while manual saving often. Then refer to the walkthrough to check if you missed any hidden area/item/quest/approach/dialogue. As this is a large game, investing in a second playthrough can be extremely time consuming. Therefore, it’s best to experience the complete buffet of game content in the very first playthrough.

[*]Another benefit of referring to a walkthrough was discovering the optimal playthrough order. That would be: PoE Act 1, PoE Act 2, White March P1, PoE Act 3, White March P2, PoE Epilogue. That approach covered all of the Definitive Edition content in a chronological manner.

[*]The dragon battles were the toughest in my opinion; the other encounters could be managed using kiting, drawing enemies to narrow corridors or springing traps or ambushes. 

[*]The game dumps a large amount of lore and history from character creation itself. Much of it didn’t make sense until Act 2 and onwards; therefore, a healthy amount of patience is required. Perhaps this was intentional as the developers had to create all this new lore and world history from scratch; certainly no easy task.

[*]Wizards are the most fun class and next would be priests. Their wide range of spells, buffs and debuffs offered the greatest opportunity for creative problem solving gameplay.

[*]Refer to an online build guide. I played as a Wild Orlan (furry), paladin, sword and shield tank built to specifications. Therefore, I had a much smoother combat experience having an incredibly durable tank character.
[/list]

So what exactly are these so-called Pillars of Eternity? For me they represent the entire world of Eora and its various mechanisms; its cycles combined with the various race’s attempts to understand those mechanisms while living their daily lives.

We got to take better care of Aloth! - Eder.
Overall Score 9/10

Pillars of Eternity, and now Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire, are the spiritual successors to the critically acclaimed series Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale. Everything those games did to push the CRPG genres forward, this game does and then some. Rather than trying to mold 2nd edition DnD to a computer game, as Baldur's Gate did, they created every mechanic to fit an isometric RPG. This change from a strict DnD adaption to an inspired creation which draws influence from DnD made for an overall better gaming experience. Let me delve into why I think so.

The dark, morose atmosphere is, admittedly, a bit of an overused concept. Mainly because most games that do this, I feel, just lean heavily on the gore and oversexualize the whole experience. Pillars of Eternity doesn't do this. The experience they craft with this game does get a bit heavy at times, the Hollowborn Crisis and all, it doesn't rely heavily on the archetypical gore that other games does. Rather, it starts off strong, and continues to add layers to the narrative, that add weight to the decisions you make throughout. Granted, I am biased toward this setting, but I feel like if more games assumed their audience was mature enough to deal with the concepts of Death, Dreams, and Religion, games as a whole would benefit.

As I've said before, the writing in this game is nothing short of phenomenal. This continues on with the companions you pick up while playing the game. Two of which surprised me with how both narratively accurate their dilemmas were, yet still abstract enough to where you, the player, can sympathize with them because the core issue they're dealing with is something reflected in our society. Without delving into spoilers, I'll just say that Grieving Mother and Durance are the most well-written companions in gaming, period.

For me, atmosphere and writing are the two pillars (heh...) of a great RPG. You can have an intensely dynamic combat system all day long, but without well-written dialogue to push the narrative along, coupled with meaningful decisions, the combat is meaningless.

In summary, If you're a fan of isometric RPGs like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale, RPGs in general, or just curious about what the conversation is about, do yourself a favor and pick this game up!

I've owned the game since its release. Every couple of years, I'd give it another shot, only to drop it shortly after reaching the first village. This year, I felt like trying again, fully expecting the same outcome. However, this time, I pushed through. I managed to get past the initial challenging dungeon and its oppressive, grim atmosphere… and then something clicked. The story started to unfold, the world's lore became increasingly vivid, and the dialogues and characters grew ever more engaging.

Let me put it this way – I adore Baldur's Gate 3 by Larian Studios and consider it one of the finest RPGs I've ever played. That said, when it comes to atmospheric density, the originality of the narrative, and the depth of the world's lore, Obsidian’s Pillars of Eternity takes a significant lead.

P.S.
The music is an absolute masterpiece.

[i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] is an isometric RPG title developed by Obsidian Entertainment. You begin your journey as an ordinary member of a caravan travelling to the town of Gilded Vale, for the reasons of your choice, but this quickly changes as the unfolding events connect you to the world of spirits. Troubled with visions of a dark future and mysterious past, you set off to find the answers to a terrifying curse, only to find more questions.

[b]THE GOOD[/b][list]
[*] I’m a sucker for a good story and [i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] delivers exactly that, with the plot revolving around sinister happenings in the region of Dyrwood that cause tragic consequences for all of its denizens. While intrigues between the gods and mortals may be a common trope in RPG genre, here it’s expanded on by the lore that’s exceptionally rich and original. The story may not be the easiest to get a full grasp on, but the superb focus on lore and plot presentation makes it absolutely special. There’s also tons of extra information about the world, its history and mystical forces that drive it, for those interested in fuller immersion.
[*] At first I was sceptical of a story DLC split into two parts, but then it turned out it was completely unfounded. Don’t be fooled by the shared title ([i]The White March[/i]) – both DLCs bring plenty of different gameplay extras. Part 1 adds a new region to explore, a storyline of an abandoned forge able to shape the world and a couple of mechanical improvements. Part 2 expands on that, as well as grants access to a couple of high-level challenges. Overall, a very strong (and long) addition, definitely worth its price. The only caveat I have is that the storyline isn’t well matched with the main game and can provide too much distraction from, you know, actually saving the world. Maybe it’s not that important after all?
[*] There’s so much stuff to do in the game you’ll have spent dozens of hours before you’re finished. An incredible asset of Pillars of Eternity is that no quest seems unsubstantial, not even the most trivial task feels forcefully shoved into the game to artificially bloat it, and your hero always feels to exist in the middle of affairs of great importance. And some of these really are important, as your choices craft your further experience with people you meet, organisations of dubious intents and events that progress your way to an inevitable clash with the ultimate evil.
[*] And speaking of choices, the game emphasises their significance through the system of reputation and personality traits, a multivariate approach to shaping the world’s responses to your actions. Each region and major organisation has its own view on your hero through separate reputation stats, allowing you to be the saviour and the villain at the same time, depending on your roleplaying needs. And consequences of treading your path reach beyond just that with the personality trait scores that increase purely based on your decisions. Gaining some traits open new options for resolving quests or dialoguing and may as well make some things harder if your interlocutor doesn’t fancy you being too honest or cruel.
[*] The classes are the shining beacon of mechanical diversity of the game. Even the RPG usuals such as the warrior or the wizard aren’t just a copy-paste of what you see in an average representative of the genre, gaining multiplicity of advancement perks and options that may lean their progress towards a satisfactorily different playstyle if that’s what you want. And then you have the bard with their chants you get to craft depending on what passive boons you need at the moment, only to strike with powerful magic once you’ve sung enough, the cipher that uses psychic abilities to easily break through the enemy’s defences, or the monk whose powers rely on getting their cheeks clapped during a fight. If you’re in for somewhat expansive mechanics that at the same time aren’t overwhelming, your playthrough may get a couple of more hours spent on checking out the available options.
[*] The stronghold is such a cool base of operations it actually needs its own point on this list. Not only you get to bring back its greatness with various upgrades, but you also get a couple of different “filler” types of content, like deciding the fates of people in the area, extra side quests for your inactive companions or getting ingredients for your alchemical shenanigans. It’s a very interesting way of expanding the game’s lore and strengthening the immersion.
[*] A lot of thought was put into the sonic presentation of the game. The music hauntingly fills the atmosphere of events and places together with thoroughly mastered sound effects, and voice actors clearly committed to their jobs as well.
[*] It’s a game tailored for a wide range of RPG fans out there. Whether you’re a casual player, a tactical mastermind or anyone in between, there’s enough gameplay settings for you to craft your ideal experience. Need an extra safeguard when your companion is about to die? No problem. Want to disable tooltips to seep more realism into your game? Sure thing. Feel like getting ultimately challenged? Try the Path of the Damned mode (and regret later!). Or go the other way around and explore the world (almost) freely with the Story Time difficulty.[/list]

[b]THE SO-SO[/b][list]
[*] There’s a good deal of dialogue option to choose from and some of them bear great importance and equally great consequences, but too many are hidden behind ridiculous stat requirements that feel almost unreachable at the current level of progress. Sometimes you can’t get back to the core of a discussion after picking an option that may have sounded completely neutral, like an innocent question before digging deeper into the topic. In a way it’s a method of preventing your hero from becoming an all-knowing Mary Sue – which is a good thing – but then you may be left with a feeling that they’re actually quite dumb for not having come up with an idea that seemed pretty obvious, but it’s locked behind a stat requirement. Also screw you, Resolve, for almost being a must pick in this department.
[*] There’s many equipment options to fit into your desired playstyle and those more gifted in figuring out mechanical details may feel at home with the ability to switch weapon sets depending on the enemy’s armour type and whatnot, but to me it all lacks the oomph. There’s a couple of powerful items you need to upgrade by meeting certain conditions (which is an interesting concept), but everything else feels rather samey. It’s not entirely bad, because you don’t need to push for the greatest rewards in order to enjoy the game, but at the same time you don’t even have to look at your inventory screen after a certain point.[/list]

[b]THE BAD[/b][list]
[*] Pathfinding is just dire. The characters seem to take up more space than what’s shown on the screen, or maybe they’re just all stupid, who knows. What I definitely know, though, is that multiple encounters ended up much worse than they could have purely because my companions struggled to move their pixel bodies to designated points, even though they really shouldn’t. If there’s two tips I can give you, one is “avoid fighting in corridors, even if they seem wide enough”…
[*] …and the other one is “practice your patience”, because that’s what’s going to be strained during loading screens. The game just loads forever. Maybe that’s the “eternity” part of the title, since I actually never figured that one out.[/list]

[b]OVERALL[/b]
[i]Pillars of Eternity[/i] takes what’s best in RPG genre and incorporates it into a unique universe. It’s packed with a really great plot, interesting events and memorable characters, as well as fun mechanics that are void of major holes. For me it was definitely more of a story-driven game than one that shines bright with its gameplay, but nonetheless it is without a doubt a worthy successor to the classics like [i]Baldur’s Gate[/i].

So I just finished the game... [Review]

Well, at 46 hours, that was one, long and fun ride.  I haven't felt so involved in a roleplaying game since Planescape : Tormet and it speaks volumes of the writing here.  There were a couple bugs and I'll get to them in an instant but the major ones were swiftly corrected, leaving some minor ones with very little impact in game.

First, let's start with the obvious.  This game was obviously developped by gamers who know what they like in a game.  Everything about the interface screams convenience.  At first I was surprised to only find sixteen equipment slots in the inventory, until I noticed a well organised, infinite "stash" box.  Every quest item and ingredient (and there's a LOT of them) instantly goes to your stash, leaving you to select only what you want to keep.  New weapon that you don't plan to use?  Stash.  Crapload of stuff on the ground?  Stash.  You can also dump equipment from your inventory to your stash if you like.  There's also an option to be able to access it anywhere, otherwise you are limited to inns and during campings.  I preferred keep it like that but it's really up to the player.

Speaking of convenience and options, there's one to enlarge the looting radius.  Basically that means that whenever you loot something from the dead, every other corpse nearby will be looted.  I definately recommend you put the radius to the maximum.  There's the usual meta-infos, what you want displayed, when the auto pause begins, there's a lot to check out.  

There's also a limited number of "resting" available, which for those abusing it in other games might come off as annoying but you get 4 on "normal" and less on harder difficulties.  You find "camping supplies" in a lot of crates and most merchants sell them as well.  By level 7, I hardly noticed the supplies since you get a lot of spells to throw to your enemies and it becomes an issue only if you're dangerously low on health.

Yes, low on health.  This is both a good and a bad thing so I won't hold the developpers for this interesting and new concept.  You have two "life" totals.  One is the stamina and the other, your actual health.  Your health is always far higher than your stamina, sometimes as much as three or four times the total and both lower at the same time.  However, since your stamina's much lower, you will fall unconscious before dying at least for a while.  After the fight, your unsconscious characters will get up and the endurance will refill quickly, up to the current health.  So when your health is low, your endurance bar will be capped and that's when you risk dying.  I thought that was an interesting idea but my issue is that the only way to raise your health is to rest.  Mind you, it does make sense in a way But there are times when you wish you didn't need to use your supplies just because one character nears death.  Even the highest priest spells do nothing to raise the health at all.  There's an option to change the final death to injuries but I left it off, I preferred the perma deaths.  Again, great work on making sure the game's tailored to a player's preferences.

On another note, I hope you love reading.  This isn't Diablo 3 here and again, I'm bringing Planescape Torment as a comparison.  The writers did a stellar job, when you can talk to a NPC, the dialogs are expansive and there's a lot of body language added for immersion.  There's also this fun idea of letting Kickstarter backers write their own NPCs.  Now and then, you'll meet people whose nameplates are golden instead of tan.  When you click on them, you can "Reach out for their souls" and get to experience, from that NPC's point of view, an important moment in their life.  They have no impact at all ingame except to give you a better immersion and let you read something fun.  I read every one I came across, some are pretty gory, others are light hearted and sweet, others just bittersweet.  It's definately an awesome way for Developpers to reward the backers and I'm pretty sure all of them bought the game just to be able to see their own NPC.  The fact that they are entirely optional is also well thought, someone who don't really like reading (and why would they play a game like that is beyond me) can just ignore them.  


Now, as far as party creation goes, I can already tell some people might feel put off by the fact you can only create one character at the start.  When you enter an Inn (and it happens within the first hour) You can hire mercenaries up to your own level, at a cost.  I found out what thanks to the generous loot, I could have a full party of six very quickly with very little impact on levels.  You also meet scripted NPCs, who are all very interesting but since my first character was a mage and the first hireable NPC you meet is also one, I went with creating my own party.  You get the standard stuff, warrior, monk, druid etc with new stuff like a chanter, which is basically a bard that can take actions while chanting and once a song is complete, you get a strong effect or a cipher who gains "mana" by damaging enemies.

I pretty much completely neglected the scripted NPCs, meaning my party never intervened or commented during conversations which was a bit sad but I did not regret it, my own party was rock solid with far better stats than the scripted ones.  By the end, I did promise myself to use the scripted ones in my next playthrought since they do offer a very lively interaction with the world.  

Very early in the game you gain a stronghold, which offers you a major questline as there's a VERY large dungeon in your own basement (actually under your own dungeon, which I thought was clever).  You can build structures to add minor bonuses when you rest at home as well as get cosmetic changes.  Overall it's a fun addition, it adds little to the overall story but again, the massive dungeon alone is worth it.  At fifteen levels, it's by far the largest in game and also by far the most interesting, each level has it's own "theme" and distinct look.

The enemies were for the most part varied but I admit I'd have wished to see less of these damn "shade" monsters, you see them from start to finish and by level 8, pose no serious threat.  The enemy AI is very good too, I was often surprised by flanking moves and concentrated attacks on vulnerable party members.

Speaking of AI, there is one, for your party, kinda.  I wish it would show a bit more initiative but once the fight begins, the party members mostly find a new target by themselves but at the start, won't do anything unless you order them to.  They also don't seek new targets if they are too far either.  Personally I like to micromanage my party so I hadn't noticed this until well into the game, as I issued my orders right from the first active pause of combat.

The game is capped at level 12.  While I understand that at this point you can easily steamroll most fights by just asking everyone to rush in, I hit that limit very early, at the start of act 3.  There's a "bounty" quest system from your fortress' lodge that are basically "go there and kill this person" and they are challenging fights but gives a LOT of XP.  Capping at 15 might have given more of an incentive to finish all quests.  The spells stop at level 6 but there's room for 3-4 more levels in the list, I figure that if the game sells well (and it sure did) they could consider that in the sequel.

Now for the auditory review...  you normally don't expect a game like that to look so good but I've paused at several times in game just to look around and admire the scenery.  Most dungeons are a feast for the eye and the music is really good.  It has a very "Obsidian" theme to it.

Verdict : 92%.  STRONGLY recommended.

Background: I discovered Pillars of Eternity in the context of finding games with similar, if not the same, "real-time party-based RPG" feel as Fallout Tactics: Brotherhood of Steel (a childhood favorite of mine). I played the game on normal difficulty and completed all main quests, side quests & tasks. As I usually play games largely for the story while setting reasonable difficulty, I don't intend to have further playthroughs with the game.

I enjoyed playing this game for almost 200 hours. The plot/story is engaging and I was pleasantly surprised when its puzzle pieces started to come together in the Final Act. The wide conversation options and the consequences stemming from them are impressive. The companions you encounter in the game enrich the experience with their takes on your journeys together. The graphics were decent, at least for its age. 

As this is only my second time playing with such a game (after Fallout Tactics), I was shocked but had fun dealing with the complex game mechanics: many classes & races, 8 damage types, 4 categories of defenses, 6 attributes with impacts that do not seem intuitive at first (e.g., a barbarian frontline crowd-control character needing high Intellect attribute for its abilities and talents to be more useful), and a lot more. To keep up with the complexities of the game, I actually had to make tables of abilities/talents/spells/chants/invocations and statistics of enemy types detailing their strengths and weaknesses. There is also a nice figure available online by user Gairnulf that details the effects of the attributes: https://pillarsofeternity.fandom.com/wiki/Attributes?file=Attribute_effects.png. All of these somehow made the game less overwhelming for me.

Perhaps the two issues (albeit minor and forgivable) I have with the game that I can think of is that (1) some of the written dialog have no voice counterpart or have a slightly different voice counterpart and (2) there are several instances when I had to read blocks and blocks of text in the game to make sense of something.

Overall, this game is a great exercise on exploring nuanced consequences of choices - from gameplay when creating your characters and allotting points to their attributes, skills, abilities, talents and spells/chants/invocations to story progression. I look forward to play Pillars of Eternity II in the future.

Alright, this is going to be a bit more in depth. So if you're interested in the mechanics featured in Pillars of Eternity, this might be for you.

[h1]Character Attributes and Stats[/h1]
Attributes as you might know them, have been repurposed, and some of their effects put into their own sub categories. Every main Attribute has it's base purpose now. Like [i]Intelligence[/i] for example affects the size of the AoE and how long spells/buffs/skills last, and [i]Might[/i] affects the strength of physical attacks, spells and also healing. 

The reason for this change is to throw away the old min/maxing of stats in favor of viability and sandbox character creation. Other effects that are usually tied to these attributes or classes have their own categories now, which can be adjusted through equipment or during a lvl up. One example of this is [i]Lore[/i]. Where [i]Intelligence[/i] is used in other games to determine what scrolls you can read, [i]Lore[/i] takes it's place in PoE. 

Even though this might sound intimidating or confusing at first, it honestly isn't. Not only is it easier to understand than the "old" way, where the same attributes affect different classes in different ways, but it also prevents hitting a wall in late game because you chose the wrong attributes for your class in the beginning. In PoE this problem is (almost) nonexistant because the system is made so your character will still be viable. Maybe not the way you planned it originally, but still viable. Even messing up deliberately is very hard to do. The basic idea is: create your character the way you want it. And the tooltips explain very clearly what each stat does and how it affects your character, making it very easy to build the one you want to play. 

[h1]Combat system[/h1]
Combat in PoE is real time with the option to pause it anytime you want. And you definitely want to pause, because the combat is generally pretty fast in this game. Most fights against regular mobs are over after the first couple of seconds if you have a strong opening(The Cipher's 'Mind Blades' followed up by crippling melee skills for example.) I've played two characters on normal and hard so far, and most basic encounters are relatively easy when using the right strategy. But a strong opening, combined with tactical positioning is the key to handle most encounters quickly. This game rewards the thinking person, and the combat is no exception. 

The combat system is quite deep and has a lot of room for tactical adjustments. I'll just cover the basics here. As you might suspect, dice play a large role in combat. If you hit your enemy or not, is determined by a D100. 1-50 is a grazed hit and 50-100 a regular hit. -0 is a miss, and +100 a critical hit. Grazed hits do -50% DMG, crits do +50%, and a miss makes you look like an idiot. Here's an example of an attack as you'll see it in the combat log: 

[b]Acc:40 - Def:26 = 14. Roll:70 + 14 = 84(Hit). 13.5 - (DR:6.0 - 3.0) = 10.5 Pierce[/b] 

So, what's happening here? First you have your [i]Accuracy[/i] which is compared to the [i]Defense[/i] of the defender. In this case the difference is 14 in my favor(40-26=14.) Next is my dice roll to which the previous result is added(or subtracted if your Acc is lower than the defender's Def.) I rolled a 70 plus the 14 from my Acc bonus, meaning 84 = a Hit!
Then, there's the DMG my weapon does(13.5) and after that the [i]]Damage Reduction[/i] from the defender, which is subtracted from my attack's DMG. Normally this would reduce my damage to 7.5(13.5-6.0), but since my Dagger has the effect to bypass 3.0 [i]Damage Reduction[/i], I only get a 3.0 penalty and do 10.5 Pierce type damage.

Whew! Not so complicated after all is it? However, there are 4 different types of Defense for each character and multiple types of Damage Reduction, which give this system quite a lot of depth to work with.

Another basic mechanic is [i]Engagement.[/i] Once two characters are engaged in combat, they are "locked" to each other. Breaking this lock[i](to escape or attack a different character)[/i] gives the other combatant a free attack. This is a fundamental system, that some people have trouble working with. It also means that the character making the most DMG or aggro doesn't necessarily pull all your enemies. This is where clever positioning and the usage of skills comes into play. (You're going to hate enemies that tunnel or warp their way around your carefully aligned defense. Stop them with spells and skills before they get a chance to do so. See: strong opening.) 

[h1]Vitality & Endurance[/h1]
Pillars of Eternity has basically two versions of Health: [i]Vitality[/i] and [i]Endurance.[/i] [i]Endurance[/i] is your resistance to short-term injury, or how much damage a character can withstand before they are knocked unconscious in battle. [i]Vitality[/i] represents long-term injury or how much damage a character can sustain before they are maimed or die permanently. A character's [i]Vitality[/i] is based on his [i]Endurance[/i] and multiplied according to his class. A [i]Druid[/i] with an End. of 50 will have Vit. of 200, since his class multiplicator is 4. 

Every hit you take in battle reduces End. & Vit. If your character takes 10DMG, you'll lose 10 End. & 10 Vit. End. is de facto your combat health, and if it's totally depleted, you're knocked out for the rest of the battle. Therefore the healing spells/skills in the game affect the End. The only way to replenish your [i]Vitality[/i] however is by resting. Either by camping or sleeping in taverns. Also, your End. will sink with your Vit. once it reaches it's value. Meaning that with a Vit. of 36, you'll also have an End. of 36. 

If your [i]Vitality[/i] reaches 0, you'll be maimed. Maimed is a serious condition that inflicts grave combat penalties. Once a character has been maimed, further reduction of Vit. will always result in death, and it can only be healed through resting.

[h1]Spell casting[/h1]
As in old Infinity Engine games, spells have limited use and need resting to replenish said uses. But Pillars of Eternity also features skills that replenish after [i]each battle.[/i] The key is to balance these two, so you'll not find yourself without spells in the middle of a dungeon. The amount of camping supplies you have also varies with each difficulty. On hard, you may find yourself run out of spells and without camping supplies right before a major battle. But this is a good example of how Pillars of Eternity handles difficulty. It not simply determines the health and strength of enemies, but the amount of management and tactics required by the player. 

[h1]The Writing[/h1]
There's not much to say here, other than that it's some of the best writing I've experienced in some time. It's not only the story of the game, and the lore[i](which is almost mandatory for a setting like this)[/i], no it's the syntax that makes it so great. Even though you have walls of text in front of you, it almost never feels bothersome to read. Language and sentences are formed so reading remains fluid at all times. Party members are full of character and always fun to interact with, and even regular NPCs are interesting, since even the most basic Q&A session is tied to a bigger story.

[h1]Bugs[/h1]
As it is tradition with Obsidian games, Pillars of Eternity suffers from some release bugs. Some common bugs are that you can't leave areas, crashes when entering a certain area, that the cursor stops working etc. All these are already confirmed to be fixed by next week though. 

Pillars of Eternity is not simply Baldur's Gate 3, and I thank Obsidian for breaking through the wall of overused mechanics, which not only enhances the game to a great deal, but also makes it truly stand out as a CRPG. Read the tooltips and get familiar with the mechanics early on, before you hit the "real" part of the game, and you won't have any trouble with frustration :^)

Pillars of Eternity is a difficult game for me to judge. On the one hand I would highly recommend it to others, especially those who enjoy detailed, morally-grey RPGs. There are a ton of different Quests, side-quests and tasks for the player to sink their teeth in to. Choices that, in other RPGs would be black & white, are not so easy here to make. The characters are well fleshed out and I thoroughly enjoyed getting to know most of them. The game itself is beautiful to look at for an isometric game, which itself harks back to Baldur's Gate. The new game system, different from DnD rules, have enough tactical depth that someone who really wanted to could spend hours diving in to to get just right.

Now on the other hand, I loved, LOVED the entire Baldur's Gate saga. I have loved everything that Obsidian at the time this game came out had created: Fallout: New Vegas, KOTOR 2, Alpha Protocol etc. So when I heard that Obsidian was making their own IP based on isometric RPGs of yore, I was so excited. I bought the entire game and the White March DLC. I played it initially for hours - and then stopped.

For me, personally, I just found that the game became a grind. The story itself was starting to drag and I couldn't get in to it the same way I did with Baldur's Gate. I wanted to love this game so much, that I kept coming back to it to try and complete it. Unfortunately, I'm not sure what it is that puts me off about the game. It could be the lack of understanding in regards to the combat; maybe my tastes have changed because of The Witcher trilogy (which I did play when the original game released, I didn't jump on the bandwagon) and Divinity: Original Sin 1 and 2; for some reason I just couldn't get in to PoE.

So why do I recommend it?

For all the reasons in the first paragraph. My own opinion shouldn't count against PoE. I know it is a great game, made by a great developer, but for me I just couldn't get in to it as much as I did with Baldur's Gate, which I continue to play to this day. Hopefully if you're a RPG fan or an Obsidian fan, you will find much love in this game.

Warning: this is going to be long (with next to no spoilers.)
I have tried PoE twice, first when it came out and then just now, some ~6 years later. First time I have tried it I lost interest and gave up on it 70+ hours afterwards, which is strange since I haven't even completed it. 
After additional ~40 hours in 2021 from scratch I ended up in the exact same state in almost the same place as the first time story-wise. The conclusion is that there is something in this game that consistently makes me eventually lose interest in it, even though at first it is very interesting, checks all the boxes and makes you play non-stop. I have tried for quite a while to understand what is wrong with it for me and from what perspective, read a lot of other reviews and now, finally, I think I'm able to formulate more or less precisely my impressions and experience with PoE.  

A few TL;DR bulletpoints:
1) Objectively - this is a very good game. Truly a labour of love with complex and original mechanics (some of them), a lot of world-building, mature topics, tons of content. I'm only pressing "NOT RECOMMEND" because Steam is black and white and in this case my "red" won't affect the rating much and will stand out more for someone with similar tastes.
2) Its complex combat mechanics and micromanagement are not for everyone. I happen to enjoy this kind of thing and played 90% of my 100+ hours on Path of the Damned difficulty. And while I will outline some criticisms below, it's not the tactical difficulty and micromanagement itself that is a problem for me, but rather the risk-reward system and how it affects progression.
3) The story itself is ok and typically Obsidianesque in its moral greyness, which I happen to be a great fan of (my favourite RPGs ever are probably Kotor 2 and NWN2:MotB.). However, I will actually critisize it as well, mostly the way the story is interacting with the player (or, rather, how it actually doesn't).
4) The game borrows A LOT of concepts from it's predecessors - mostly Baldur's Gate series. Art style, interface(s), pausable pseudo-real time combat mechanics, e.t.c. In fact, even the music at times feels almost a plagiarism, with not just a hint of BG1/2 but like a remix or cover version. Most of these mechanics and borrowed concepts, to be fair, have been improved in PoE. However, for me there is a general feeling of "borrowed too much, simply for the sake of nostalgia and homage to predecessors, borrowed unnecessary and clunky things".

So, points 2 to 4 in more detail now:
2) I won't go on about attributes and how they work and that it's not very logical (Might both for wizards and fighters e.t.c). Every game has its rules and their "realism" is a matter of convention anyway. The system works overall and it's weirdness (or originality, however you want to put it) wasn't enough to deter me from playing. What I mentioned is a risk-reward problem that I see with the game. If you are in the zone roughly corresponding to your character level and are playing on a higher difficulty - chances are there won't be any really easy fights. In and of itself this isn't bad at all (if I wanted easy I'd play the story mode), but what is wrong, IMO, is the fact that it affects overall pacing too much. Quite simply - I feel bored and don't want to clear out a side-map, because I will receive almost nothing in return. I think limiting XP from monster kills was a big mistake from the devs. It prevents farming for XP, yes, but it also makes huge parts of maps filled with unnecessary and completely unrewarding fights. The way loot and items work in this game, most of those fights hardly yield anything valuable either. Simply put - there's almost no incentive exploring quest-unrelated areas, as I'm just going to waste time for nothing. There is no sense of accomplishment or dopamine reward in winning those tough-ish fights number 7 in some shithole number 10 at the end of nowhere. The sense of wanting to explore every nook and cranny of the map just isn't there for me - too much time, too little gain, too much repetition of the same on nearly any map.

3) The story, while in itself quite interesting, has one major flaw: it doesn't really push you to interact with it. The premise is unmotivating: you become a Watcher, what exactly is a Watcher is not explained to you beyond the fact that you can now see and talk with souls. Somehow, regardless of your own reaction to this development, your character will want to stop being a Watcher in all relevant dialogues. Eventually it is revealed that being a Watcher might (unclear if for sure or not) drive you insane. This is supposed to give some legitimacy to your (forced upon you by the game) desire to stop being a Watcher, but since no game mechanic actively pushes you to do anything about it, it just looks really strange and illogical. In MotB the game MAKES you either want to master your spirit-eating or get rid of it, it actively tries to kill you or something around you. In BG2 you sometimes turn into a rampaging abomination and will slowly lose your identity and soul if you don't progress through the plot. Again - this is always a convention, there are a lot of jokes about games that seem to impart great importance and urgency to your progress through the main quest, but you can still waste dozens of hours doing completely unrelated stuff with no consequences (Skyrim, or Geralt in Witcher 3 going around playing Gwent or fist-fighting instead of searching for Ciri). There has to be balance between the two and I think PoE fails in this regard - it takes a too much laid back approach to pushing the player onwards. In fact, I think even Endless Paths of Od Nua subquest does a better job of urging you to explore the depths, as your keep might eventually be in real physical danger (at least it is said so and there are some random attacks from below in the keep mini-game). The issue isn't helped by the fact that the main antagonist (always extremely important for any engaging story) absolutely doesn't care about you and the game doesn't really make you care about him either. So he accidentally made you a Watcher - so what? Well, you can now walk around, click on half of the characters on each map and read a wall of purple prose that affects you or anyone or anything else in exactly no way at all. I wonder if there is anyone who read through all of that and actually found it interesting past a first couple of them. I feel truly bad for writers who put so much work into those mini-stories, because the way the game handles them just basically guarantees 95% of that work will just never be appreciated at all. The game doesn't make you care about it. It's there if you want it - but why would you if it is made clear it is all completely unrelated?
And so you're stuck between the story that doesn't make you do anything about it, through neither emotional nor physical connection - and exploration that eventually just gets tedious, boring and unrewarding. I think, in the end - this is precisely the trigger that made me give up on the game twice.

4) It is almost as if they thought "in order to be successful, the game must look, feel, play and sound exactly like Baldur's Gate 2". Why would you copy extremely clunky BG inventory - and then add bottomless stash to which you can teleport items or teleport them back to you only if you rest (in the wild - wasting a precious camping resource of which on higher difficulties you only have 2). And for what - you can just travel to any safe location and access it there anyway, there are no dangerous ambushes or random encounters in between maps in this game. For some reason the very thing that made travelling meaningful and dangerous in - WASN'T copied. Why is there a keep managing mini-game in PoE? Simply because you had the same in BG2 and NWN2?

I have given thumbs-up to both postive and negative reviews of Pillars. This is a hit or miss game; for me personally, it was nearly a miss on more than one occasion. Yet there was enough for me to keep playing, all the way to the end. At certain points I was drawn in; this is what the best games do, but all things told, Pillars of Eternity is not an exceptional game. 

To me, Pillars is the Buick of the RPG world. It won't blow you away, but it will get you where you need to go. It excels in character development, skills, spells, and game mechanics. It looks good (though not spectacular), and has well designed levels. 

There is an interesting story here, but it is oddly difused. Ultimately it's marred by an inability to relate to the characters. This I believe has a lot to do with the same small static face for each main character (and no face at all for many of the NPC's) regardless of the dialogue. 

What does Pillars of Eternity add to the genre? Well, there was a lot of hype which renewed interest. There is nothing remotely revolutionary though. The sense of wonder, excitement, adventure is mostly absent. Exploration of new maps and the never-ending search for good loot works well here. 

My thumbs-up is indeed a rather luke-warm one, but is not unearned. I've played RPG's since the days of FFIII and Phantasy Star 2, and of course Baldaur's Gate. But if this is one's first foray into the genre, it's difficult to predict if you'll like it or not. 

Pillars of Eternity may be a Buick of RPG's, but it's a brand-new shiny one, with lots of mileage in it. If you are a fan of the genre, give it a try.

Obsidian Entertainment’s Pillars of Eternity was the highest funded Kickstarter game of 2012 with almost four million dollars raised. Originally called Project Eternity, it beckoned a new age for isometric RPGs in the tradition of the Infinity Engine games such as Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale and Planescape: Torment. This age is now consolidated by several other isometric or just plain old school RPGs released and announced since then, and, in many ways, Pillars was a pioneering game that revitalised the genre.

As the creation of an entirely new IP with all that it entails in worldbuilding, lore and ruleset, Pillars is quite unique. Whereas the Infinity Engine games were based on D&D, Pillars took inspiration from D&D, the games based on it, and several new fantasy tropes and sources to create an entirely new world. The character creation process is rather overwhelming because of this, but now, equipped with the accumulated knowledge of the fan community and several balancing and optimisation patches, there are many possibilities to create a wide range of different character builds, and that’s just accounting for races and classes.

Pillars stands apart by building upon the foundation of classic RPG fantasy, but not in a generic way that just rehashes the same old tropes. Whereas Baldur’s Gate and Icewind Dale were more traditional medieval fantasy RPGs, Pillars is more like a “renaissance fantasy” RPG, which includes primitive firearms and several other details that make for a less hackneyed setting. And I for one am bored to death of Tolkien-styled elves and dwarves, so the fact that Pillars offers three unique races (Aumaua, Orlan, and Godlike) makes a lot of difference and adds enough replay value to justify several playthroughs. And even if you replay it a couple of times with those new races, you will find that there will be much you missed in other ways.

On the other hand, there are also plenty of comfortable tropes in the sense that the player character is a Watcher, another variety of The Chosen One, and in that sense it plays like a very typical classic fantasy RPG. As a Watcher you can see and speak to souls, either those lingering in certain obscure places, or in some living bodies, or as fragments of souls left in objects and corpses. Combined with a dark fantasy trope where some children are born without souls, it makes for a compelling initial setting that will engage the player even through overwhelming lore dumps of the cosmological and metaphysical variety.

There is a certain fascination in untangling the details of events and the backstories of the companions you pick up along the way, but it does involve a great amount of reading that will likely alienate a lot of players. While you can avoid most of it and focus simply on the combat to “beat” the game, you will miss most of what makes it a unique RPG. Min-maxing your way to a quick resolution will probably leave you totally clueless about what exactly you are doing and how your actions and decisions will impact the game world.

As an overall experience, Pillars has the usual pros and cons of old school RPGs. Beautiful environment art, but the character art and animation do look dated now. The soundtrack is nothing special, but also not bad at all. Voice acting ranges from great to boring, patchy and drawn-out at times. The writing can be verbose and overly florid sometimes, but in general it’s mature and profound, requiring an investment in putting the pieces together.

At a certain point in the game you will be required to choose a faction in Defiance Bay, and this was rather poorly handled in quest design. There is zero implication that the faction quests are conflicting at all until you find yourself having to be sponsored by one of them into the ducal palace hearings. At most you might get a sense that you are stepping on the toes of other factions, which you could interpret as simply a loss in reputation. Obsidian has done tremendously well with faction quest design in the past, more notably in Fallout: New Vegas, so it’s rather strange that in Pillars it plays so carelessly.

Character customisation is very deep, very detailed and very balanced. The RPG system and ruleset, inspired mostly by D&D 4E, will take some getting used to by newcomers, and it could have been better handled in the way of skills and skill checks, but it does reward the player who invests time in learning the inner workings beyond min-maxing to explore a variety of playstyles and builds.

Even if you love real-time with pause combat, it can get very frustrating on higher difficulties, and the AI pathfinding can be horrible, with the characters sometimes wiggling back and forth trying to find a spot to reach at an opponent, looking very glitchy and poorly developed. Unless you bottleneck the opponent into handling your melee characters while your rangers and magic users get them from behind, expect messy and annoying battles, especially if you try to keep your companions alive to see their quests through.

And though there are some great stories told by the writers through the companions, the interactions with them are more limited and linear than one would expect, given the clear influence of Planescape: Torment, which is probably the best classic Infinity Engine game in terms of companion engagement and interactions. Both Torment and Pillars are equally verbose, but Torment has far superior interactivity and reactivity.

The writing suffers particularly when there are too many cases of ornate made-up words where regular words would have served equally well. This often makes reading a chore, having to keep up with the vocabulary that props up a supposedly peculiar element or detail that is not always that peculiar. Then again, you don’t have to read it, but for those who do enjoy reading and exploring worldbuilding in games, some patience will be required in that regard.

Technically speaking, it can be a cumbersome game, with sprawling levels where you have to drag your characters back and forth, scrolling the map over and over to get to the transition points. And the loading screens are way too frequent and too slow for such an undemanding game in terms of performance. Even on an SSD, it felt like it dragged on and on for almost a minute, often to load just a small level. While the game has seen a lot of optimisation in terms of ruleset balance, performance remains a bit of a drag.

It also has some of the hardest achievements in the history of achievements. These are actual achievements, not just milestones that can’t be missed if you finish the main quest. The Path of the Damned difficulty mode is a spiritual successor of Icewind Dale’s Heart of Fury mode, and it makes combat much more brutal, requiring more expertly crafted min-maxed builds to even consider it.

In terms of sheer bang for your buck, Pillars is a bargain, especially now. Sure, you can “beat” it in under 10 hours even in the hardest difficulty, but this approach to “beating” the game is pointless because this is a game where it’s not about the destination, it’s about the journey and the details of worldbuilding, lore and character development you pick up along the way. As you soak it all in, little by little, you will find this is a monumental achievement in worldbuilding that few other developers could have managed, though it feels overwhelming and overelaborate at times. And that’s what makes Pillars of Eternity stand the test of time.

I finally finished this game after having it for years.

It has a special feeling I don't get from other games. It's mysterious and a little strange. The writing and the big ideas in the story make you really think. It feels less like winning a game, and more like finishing a powerful book that stays with you.

And a big part of why I loved it was my favorite companion, Eder. He's a simple farmer turned soldier, with his easy humor and down-to-earth wisdom. his back and forth talking with Iselmyr makes for a pretty hilarious journey XD 

try this game at least once in your life , you won't regret it

Divinity 2 may be a more polished game gameplay-wise, but there's something about the art style, lore, and music in this game that grabs me. Where some CRPG's aim to recreate the feeling of playing D and D, this game makes me feel like I am playing through a Tolkien novel. I know some people are put off by the lack of voiced dialogue but the writing in this game is superb in my opinion and I enjoy reading it. I had played Wasteland 2 and the original Divinity before this game, but this was the game that made me appreciate the CRPG genre the most.

It's a fun game. Definitely reminiscent of games like Icewind Dale, Baldur's Gate 1&2. The mechanics and rules are different but similar, I think neither adding nor subtracting from the game, just requiring familiarization. I thoroughly enjoyed the game and found there are days and days of content, if not weeks and weeks. 

I did not really encounter any bugs that I can think of, I can't think of a time I was stopped from playing and frustrated by an obvious flaw or bug. 

I got enjoyment from both nostalgia for similar games from years, decades ago, and the sense of D&D style adventure and discovery, and the merit of the game itself and it's own storylines and exploration and battles. I REALLY liked that there is some light upgrading, crafting, and your own fortress and home base. That to me added another level that I don't remember from Icewind or Baldur. Having my own castle/home base, with hirelings and different rooms and local merchants, was a nice added touch. IMO that kind of thing added to any game, really gives you a sense of living in the world, like homes in Skyrim, and other games. And it does kind of give you a sense that you are escaping to your own world, with your own home, where you get a satisfaction of comfort and belonging.

So I can't really think of any negatives, and can only say I felt this is solid gaming and entertainment, worth the price.

What an experience. The lore, combat, and other mechanics were really overwhelming at the start, but once I got into it, it became so much fun to play. I absolutely love the Divinity Original Sins series and looked at pillars as another game in the genre I could sink my teeth into after finishing the two games in the series. I definitely think original sins is way sleeker, more modern, and easier to get into than pillars but once you get past the slightly older looking graphics and master the play-pause combat, everything opens up to you. The story is extremely rich, well-written, and well-voiced. There were parts of the story that gave me chills, and I felt like I was in the game making choices I would make if I were in those situations. It really is an incredible role-playing experience. With Baldur's Gate III on the horizon, I'm excited now to go back to play Baldur's Gate I and II, which heavily inspired pillars. [h1] What I liked in PoE? [/h1]

First of all, from the first hours in game you understand, that you are dealing with a top notch game. Straight from the character creation screen, where you can choose from multiple familiar races mixed with some you’ve never seen before. Then when it goes to classes, man, it’s one of the most stressful times for me, especially in a games like PoE. I always feel like, damn is that class OP? Am I going to feel good playing him? Should I google for some builds, etc? That’s usually the place, where I can stuck for hours thinking and reconsidering. In PoE it was even more harder, because after looking for polls and opinions regarding best class I understood that there is no such thing like the best one in here and you should stick with the one, which gameplay style fits you the best. Next, I was a bit confused by the idea of choosing the right spells for you. You know, like most of the time, I tend to play such games where you just pick a character/class that looks good for you and it has its own set of spells, abilities, talents which you can improve one way or another along the game. In PoE you have to choose your starter spells/talents to make your own ultimate warmachine and this can make you feel a bit uncomfortable at first, but then when you start to play you understand how great this idea is.

After all these hours of choosing your class, you actually start playing the game. From the first minutes of the game you understand that you dealing with a dark atmospheric RPG where you will be mainly focused on reading a lot of dialogues and bestiaries to learn as much as possible about the game’s lore. This feature however has an opposite effect. I mean like, I really like to fully dive in game, learning everything about its rich story, characters and history of the magical world, but when you have to read THAT much it can burn you quickly. 

You are playing as a Watcher - a person who can read the souls of person around them, by touching it. It can be both living and dead one, doesn’t matter, the fact that you will use that feature alongside the game to get the insight about character’s stories and motives. The game starts with a bit of a WOW-effect (no spoilers here) and you have to learn about your new ability and find your answers. This is where your adventure starts and where you begin to meet a lot of different characters with their own stories. Some of them will be willing to join you so they can battle with you on your side and this will open new stories and quests for you which will lead you to new adventures. In general, I can say that PoE is a big adventure, where you will be traveling the world from one map to another, searching for a new quests, trying to speak with every character possible just to know a little bit more about the world’s lore and secrets to reveal. It surely has its own main story, that will guide you through the game showing where to go next and guiding you through adventure, but it’s definitely up to you either you wanna rush through it asap or enjoy the whole story with its side quests and your companions stories. 

Overall, the narrative part in game is pretty much strong. Pretty much similar as in other games of this genre a new dialogue options will unlock depends on lots of different factors - your race, class, abilities, how much strength, might or intelligence you have. 

[h1] Okay, I got it, you like this game and you are trying to sell it, but I am pretty much sure, there was something you didn’t like about it, what was that? [/h1]

It’s a good question. Because, PoE surely has its own cons and things to hate. Something that will make you hate it at some point. First of all, I’d like to say that this castle thing was a completely redundant in game. During the first act you will find a castle and from this point you will need to build it, improve it, add new buildings and invest in it as much as possible. I was really enjoying my quests, tracking storyline and just having fun exploring the world and then I started to get all these annoying messages regarding my castle that it was under attack. You can solve it automatically, but you will most likely fail and lose some of the buildings, so you will have to invest to them once again and the game forces you to solve it by yourself traveling to the castle, wasting a lot of time. Another thing that really annoyed me, that during the lack of investment and that game was backed by fans mostly, it feels like they wasn’t able to voice every dialogue in game. That’s pretty much it! I can say, that PoE is a great product, which can satisfy the RPG lover’s needs and bring old memories back to the surface. [b]Pillars of Eternity[/b] is the best roleplaying game I've played since Neverwinter Nights.

It's a classical western fantasy RPG - the player guides a party of adventurers through an epic journey, where the fate of the world just might hang in the balance.

It's clear that Pillars draws heavy inspiration from Dungeons & Dragons - when creating a character, the player chooses a race and class, then assigns attributes and skills, and the game mechanics are obviously supported by a rigid ruleset and powered by virtual dice rolls. In addition, some of the classes, weapons, etc. may be familiar to D&D aficionados, but Obsidian has done an outstanding job of creating a distinct, vibrant world for Pillars of Eternity, from a wide variety of races and (orthogonal, in some cases) cultures to a range of traditional and innovative classes to geography and folklore to political rivalries to its own pantheon of living deities, around which the main storyline revolves.

Many of the reviews of this game mention Baldur's Gate, and with good reason - gameplay-wise, Pillars borrows heavily from BG: isometric perspective, formation-oriented party management, fast-paced realtime combat with a variety of conditional autopause settings, even the "You must gather your party before venturing forth" message when transitioning between areas. However, these are all good things ([i]maybe not the message[/i]), and everything feels right, whether exploring the wilderness,  creeping anxiously through a crypt, navigating a bustling city, or frantically trying to survive an ambush. I particularly enjoyed an original mechanic they've added: there are several sections where the player is guided through a sort of illustrated choose-your-own-adventure sequence, where the various options may involve intuition, tactics, or skill checks, and will almost certainly have nontrivial consequences.

I do have a few minor quibbles: for example, it's possible to accept at least one of the optional quests and get fairly entangled in it before realizing that there's no hope of completing it at the party's current level. Each entry or exit from even the most insignificant building involves a loading screen, which means that exploring new town or village becomes a long sequence of these screens, divided by short segments of walking between buildings. Finally, the player, through a special ability she gains early on, is able to gain insight into the lives of many of the non-playable characters - however, these insights have absolutely no impact on the game in any way.

The story is epic, complex, and engaging - one of the finest I've encountered in a computer RPG, and the personas and backstories of the auxiliary playable characters the player will encounter on her travels weave seamlessly in, enriching the depth and color of the experience.

All in all, Pillars of Eternity is a fantastic game, and I would unhesitatingly recommend it to any roleplaying enthusiast.

After more than 2,100 hours with Pillars of Eternity, I can confidently recommend it to anyone who enjoys classic isometric RPGs such as Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment.

The world of Eora is rich, believable, and full of memorable lore. Combat rewards planning rather than button mashing, and character creation is among the best in the genre. Nearly every class feels unique, making repeated playthroughs genuinely worthwhile. I've created everything from druids and ciphers to paladins, priests, rangers, monks, and rogues, and each has offered a different experience.

The writing is excellent, the companions are memorable, and the soundtrack perfectly complements the atmosphere. The game also respects player choice, allowing role-playing to meaningfully shape conversations and quests.

It isn't perfect. The rules can be intimidating for newcomers, and combat can become chaotic until you learn how the systems work. The pacing is deliberate, so players looking for a fast-paced action RPG may find it slow.

Even so, these are minor criticisms compared to what the game accomplishes. Pillars of Eternity captures the spirit of the Infinity Engine classics while building an identity of its own. More than a decade after release, I still find myself starting new characters, experimenting with different builds, and discovering details I overlooked before.

If you enjoy thoughtful role-playing games with deep mechanics, excellent world-building, and tremendous replay value, this is an easy recommendation.

Ah, Pillars of Eternity…You know, the more I play RPG titles, the more I understand just one thing: I am a masochist. And I am already a lost case in many ways. I have played Baldur’s Gate on all kinds of difficulty, completed all possible tasks in Neverwinter Nights 1 and 2, died a lot in Icewind Dale, survived in the harsh world of Fallout 1, 2, and Tactics (also 3 and New Vegas, but it is a story for another day), developed my perfect kingdom in Pathfinder: Kingmaker, and found other ways to torture my poor nerves. Now, having spent 80 hours with Pillars, I only reinforced my belief that I enjoy making my life difficult – at least in games.

 Anyway, there are a lot of things that I would like to tell you about regarding this particular game. There are many controversial points that I still do not know what to think about, as well as features that I thoroughly enjoyed. Let me start with a short list first:

[u][b]Pros[/b][/u]
[list]- A fascinating world;[/list]
[list]- An engaging story with lots of twists, choices, and sudden turns; [/list]
[list]- A great variety of quests and things to do;[/list]
[list]- Very interesting character-building mechanics;[/list]
[list]- Pleasant music;[/list]
[list]- The true feeling of old-school RPGs;[/list]
[list]- Soulbound weapons;[/list]
[list]- The White March DLCs;[/list]
[list]- Dragons![/list]

[u][b]Cons[/b][/u]
[list]- A complicated pre-battle system;[/list]
[list]- Siege of Crägholdt and its annoying battles before the keep;[/list]
[list]- Those hecking dragons!!![/list]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1846777143

[u]A bit more about pros and cons[/u]

I am mostly a casual player, to be honest. I do not like monumental challenges, hopeless battles, and tasks that require hours and hours of fruitless retrying just to get one small reward. My forte is exploring and collecting. If there are two hundred quests, I will complete all of them. I will have an ultimate treasury that will contain every possible weapon from every corner of the world. Any people to save? Just call me! So, Pillars of Eternity was a great source of entertainment. There are lots of interesting books to find and read, people to meet, and places to discover. Rich lore is waiting for you at every corner, and almost every NPC has something to say. I love worlds that have their own unique settings, history, and religion. It is such a pleasure to explore them! This is the charm of classic isometric RPGs. The DLCs – The White March – opened a new part of this fantasy world and brought to light a very touching and sad story about love, duty, and betrayal. Even fantasy gods have their ups and downs, as it turns out.

Your adventure will be full of amusing events and difficult battles. You will never have problems finding what to do as the story brings you new challenges and puzzles in every chapter and location. Oh, by the way! I absolutely loved the idea of Soulbound weapons. This a unique feature that introduced new tasks and bonuses. 

Another thing worth mentioning: character classes and general development. Some of them were quite new for me, so I spent additional time learning about them. Who is a Chanter? Is it just a simple bard or something more? And what about Ciphers? And even the common classes have something new to present. Frankly speaking, I am still not really good at the whole character-building system in this game, so I had to use video guides by NerdCommander. I cannot recommend them enough: the guy knows his stuff! I am pretty sure he saved my playthrough more than once.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1846775947

Now, what can I complain about? First, compared to many other RPGs I have played, Pillars of Eternity has a very lackluster system of pre-battle preparations. If you are not a stranger to Baldur’s Gate or Neverwinter, you should know the drill by heart: before any fight your cleric uses tons of spells to enhance your party’s skills, stats, and abilities; your mage should cast something to protect weaker characters against magic; your ranger can buff their pet. Do not know the right spell? Use a scroll. And lots, tons, billions of potions! Pillars of Eternity restricts your every move in this sphere: hardly anything can be used outside of battles. The best you can do is to throw a fireball or get several points in your skills by drinking a potion. Even Clerics cannot do anything useful except for some tiny improvements or minor attacks. To my mind, it is ridiculous to buff yourself only during the battle and not before it. If you know for sure that the whole location will be full of lava and fire monsters, why would you mindlessly go there without a fire-protection spell? Yes, of course, we have food and…erm…prostitutes, but it is not exactly the same thing. Also, it is not really nice that there is only one way to restore health, not to mention that the whole health/endurance system was not a pleasant thing during the fight. Dying just because there is not even a single potion or scroll to restore your health? Really?!

Second, my particular nightmare: Siege of Crägholdt. This quest made me furious in more ways than any other. In particular, battles before the keep. Can you imagine enemies that can sense your casters from literally other side of the map? Well, here we have them a plenty! I had a fighter and two paladins in my team who were always sent headfirst into any battles and should have attracted more than enough attention. But no! Soldiers did not even notice them. They ran right to my poor wizard and utterly destroyed him with several precise hits. He was not even involved in the battle! Just standing several meters away and reading a book. This honestly infuriated me to no end and I eventually had to leave Alot far away from any fighting to save his life. The same happened with my cleric and cipher later.

And the last but not least, my most controversial thoughts are all about dragons. On the one hand, I adore them. Hardly ever will you find such a diverse selection in an RPG game: a stunningly beautiful Sky Dragon, a marvelous Adra Dragon, a cruel Alpine Dragon, and other curious species. Each design was unique. But as far as fighting is concerned…oh my God, that was so difficult! The battle with Adra Dragon took me an hour, and I do not even want to tell you how many times I had to restart this encounter before I eventually managed to deal with the threat. These creatures play dirty, and you will need all your skills to defeat such mighty opponents. Now let us also remember that there is hardly any way to use skills, potions, and spells before any battle. So your only saving grace is the brothel, no matter how funny or ridiculously it sounds. Well, at least this is yet another unique gameplay feature worth praising, I guess?
